CHAPTER-VII
ISSUES RAISED AND OBSERV ATIONS OF COMMITTEE
7.1 The Committee notes that two diametrically opposite views have emerged on the Bills. One
group strongly supported the Bills and emphasized for early passage of the Bills and conferment
of Sixth Schedule status to Darjeeling Hill areas, whereas another group with overwhelming
majority among those who appeared before the Committee, vehemently opposed the Bills and the
grant of Sixth Schedule status to the areas. The Committee also notes that both groups claimed
that there would be law and order problem if their viewpoints were ignored.
7.2 It was suggested to the Committee that the Bills should be passed and the events that may
unfold could be handled later on according to the circumstances. It was also suggested that instead
of conferring Sixth Schedule status, the Council could be given more power and autonomy and the
solution should be found within the State of West Bengal. According to them, the spirit of the
Constitution was being changed by giving Sixth Schedule status to Darjeeling, and a new precedent
was being created by extending the Schedule to an area beyond the NE region. It was further
apprehended that in future it would have to be extended to other areas as the tribal areas of Orissa,
Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Andhra Pradesh and Bihar may demand Sixth Schedule status. The
Committee also notes the fact that there are already such resolutions from Arunachal Pradesh and
Manipur and such demand may gain momentum.
7.3 The Committee notes the considered view of the Law Secretary on the issue of judicial
scrutiny and legal sustainability of the Bill. According to him, Article 244 does not anywhere say
that the Sixth Schedule is only confined to tribal areas and constitutionally there is no problem in
extending it to West Bengal. The Committee also notes the views of the Home Secretary that the
resolutions of Arunachal Pradesh and Manipur Governments were under consideration and would
be considered in the light of other factors. He does not foresee opening of the Pandora’s Box if
the Sixth Schedule status is given to Darjeeling and he was quite sure in his own assessment.
However, the Committee is not convinced by the assertions of the Home Secretary.
7.4 The Committee also takes note of the viewpoint of both the State Government as well as
the Home Secretary that those, who are opposing the Bills, are splinter groups, who had been
together with the original party when the resolution for conferring Sixth Schedule status to the
Council was adopted. It was further pointed out that as elections had not been held since long,
it was difficult to assess who enjoyed the majority. The Committee is, however, not convinced by
the reasons given by the representatives of Government of West Bengal and the Home Secretary
for not holding elections since 1999 and for the delay in bringing forward the Bills. Home
Secretary’s assumption and the Chief Secretary’s observations that those who are opposing the Bills
are fence sitters and they will fall in line once the Bills are passed and elections are held, could
have been verified had the Committee visited DaIjeeling to assess the ground reality. The
Committee observes that if the Bills had been passed immediately after signing of MoS, the
situation would have been different because Shri Ghisingh was the undisputed leader at that
time. During the last two years, much water has flown down and non-holding of election has
added fuel to the fire.
7.5 The Committee cannot be oblivious to the opposition by the overwhelming majority of the
representatives those appeared before it who asserted time and again that there would be bloodshed
24

25
in the region if the Bills are passed. At the same time, the Committee cannot also ignore the official
viewpoint that if the Bills are not passed there would be chaos, unrest and agitation. The
Committee has no mechanism at its disposal to find out the ground reality except depending
on the official stand of the Central and State Governments. Had the Committee visited the
area, it could have felt the pulse of the people. The Committee therefore, observes that it
has no option but to go by what the Government tells it in regard to the prevailing situation
or possible future law and order situation.
7.6 The Committee notes the submission of the Home Secretary that the first tripartite
discussions took place in 2001 when it was inter-alia decided that the DGHC would sent its
proposal through the State Government for its inclusion into the Sixth Schedule. But for some
reasons, it took a long time. When the tripartite agreement was signed, people were aware of it
and a lot of representations mainly on the issue of reservation for Scheduled Castes were received
which were examined by the Central Government in consultation with the State Government. The
State Government was of the opinion that it would not be appropriate to disturb the consensus
which had been arrived at after prolonged interaction and deliberation. According to the Home
Secretary, as a result of prolonged dialogue of over 20 years, two things had emerged; one was
that the Statehood demand not accepted and two the best solution after considering various options
has been to include the Council under the Sixth Schedule. He also asserted that if the whole matter
was reopened, as people are opposing, the situation may become more serious.
7.7 The Committee also notes that one of the options discussed was to insert Article 371J in
Part XXI of the Constitution. Regarding giving of special status under Fifth Schedule, the
Committee has been given to understand that this was neither discussed nor contemplated.
According to the Home Secretary special status under Fifth Schedule would have been totally
confined to the Tribal Advisory Council only and the Fifth Schedule solution would not have been
appropriate for Darjeeling Hill areas. The Law Secretary supplemented that the Fifth Schedule does
not offer any autonomy in the real sense and there are no law making powers available to the
Tribal Council.
7.8 In the context of the issue raised by Shri Ghisingh concerning working of international
spying network in the sensitive area which is called the “chicken neck” of the country, the
Committee notes the following submission of the Home Secretary:—
“In so far as any training etc. or the international espionage ring is concerned, all I
can say is that the Government is continuously looking at every such kind of possibilities
wherever they may be and we do not have any specific information of this kind. I can
assure you that if there is any information of that kind, it shall be seriously and promptly
act upon.”
7.9 One school of thought pleaded for Gorkhaland on the argument that the trend in our polity
is of creating smaller States and if smaller States like Uttarakhand, Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh can
be created to the satisfaction of those regions, Gorkhaland can also be carved out. The Committee
in this regard would like to clarify that the issue of a separate State of Gorkhaland is not its brief
and it will restrict itself to the examination of the Bills. A overwhelmingly large number of people,
who deposed before the Committee, were against the Bills and wanted Gorkhaland. But the
Committee is bound by the mandate given to it which precludes it from making its
recommendations on any matter outside the scope of the Bills.
7.10 The Committee observes that ‘Police’ and ‘Public Order’ are the responsibilities of
State Government and the Committee enquired several times both from the State
Government as well as Central Government as to whether the law and order would not
deteriorate with the passage of the Bills because the evidence before it was to the contrary.

26
Representatives of both Governments have asserted more than once that the enactment of
the Bills would not lead to any major law and order problem and rather the local people
would in course of time join the mainstream of electoral politics.
7.11 The Committee after taking into consideration the statements made by the Union
Home Secretary and the Chief Secretary, Government of West Bengal before it to the effect
that as per their assessment the passage of the Bills would fulfil the aspirations of people
of Darjeeling; they would in course of time participate in the electoral process under the
new dispensation of the Sixth Schedule; and that there would be no serious law and order
problem in Darjeeling consequent upon the passage of the Bills by Parliament and that the
apprehensions of civil unrest and turmoil in the hills in the event of conferment of the
Sixth Schedule status were highly exaggerated and in view of the lack of any mechanism
with the Committee to verity the averments of the authorities, it had no other option but
to rely on the official statements and decided to proceed with the clause-by-clause
consideration of the Bills. In this context the Committee would like to caution and advise
the Ministry of Home Affairs to make a fresh assessment of the ground realities all over
again before proceeding with the Bills in the two Houses of Parliament.

8.6 Sixth Schedule to the Constitution (Amendment) Bill 2007:
Clause 2
8.6.1 The Committee took up clause 2 of the Bill. Sub-clause (3) of clause 2 provides for
insertion of following proviso in paragraph 1, after sub-paragraph (2) of the Sixth Schedule:—
“Provided that nothing in this sub-paragraph shall apply to the areas under the
Gorkha Hill Council, Darjeeling in the State of West Bengal”.
8.6.2 Sub-paragraph (2) in paragraph 1 of Sixth Schedule provides that if there are different
Scheduled Tribes in an autonomous district, the Governor may, by public notification, divide the
area inhabited by them into autonomous regions. The Committee noted that by adding the special
proviso, the power of the Governor would be restricted. The Committee wanted to know the
necessity of the proviso and the implications thereof.
27

28
8.6.3 In response to the query of the Committee, the MHA in their written comments stated as
under:
“Sub-paragraph (1) of paragraph 1 of the Sixth Schedule makes provisions about
autonomous districts for tribal areas enumerated in the table appended to paragraph 20 of
the Schedule. Sub-paragraph (2) of paragraph 1 makes provision enabling the Governor to
divide such area or areas into autonomous regions if there are different Scheduled Tribes
in an autonomous district. Sub-paragraph (1) of paragraph 2 makes provision for the
composition of District Councils in terms of the total number of elected and nominated
members.
These provisions have remained unaltered with reference to Autonomous Hill Councils
in respect of various areas which have been constituted under the Sixth Schedule to the
Constitution from time to time. However in the case of the Bodoland Territorial Council,
the following two distinctive pr ovisions were made:—
(i) a provision was made whereby nothing in sub-paragraph (2) of paragraph 1
would apply to the Bodoland Territorial Areas District; and
(ii) specific provision was made in sub-paragraph (1) of paragraph 2 through a
proviso indicating the composition of the Council which was different from the
general composition stipulated in sub-paragraph (1) of paragraph 1.
These changes were necessitated on account of the fact that the decision to include
the areas of Bodoland Territorial Areas District had been arrived at as a part of an Accord
in which, inter alia, the specific territories to be covered and the composition of the
Council were also decided.
In the case of the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council also the proposal to bring it under
the Sixth Schedule follows Tripartite discussions between Government of India,
Government of West Bengal and Shri Subash Ghisingh (President, GNLF and Administrator,
DGHC) and a Memorandum of Settlement in which specific provisions were made
pertaining to the area to be brought under the Council (which was part of the District of
Darjeeling) and the composition of the Council. Keeping this in view similar provisions as
in the case of the Bodoland Territorial Council have been made with reference to non-
application of sub-paragraph (2) of paragraph 1 of the Sixth Schedule.
The underlying logic is that where, on the basis of an Accor d or Settlement specific
provisions regarding the area and composition of the Council have been made in the
Constitution, the existing provision in sub-paragraph (2) of paragraph 1 enabling the
Governor to divide such area or areas into autonomous regions would no longer be required”.
8.6.4 In view of the clarification given by the Ministry of Home Affairs, sub-clause (3) is
adopted.
8.7.1 The Committee then took up sub-clause (4) of clause 2, which seeks to insert following
proviso after sub-paragraph (1) in paragraph 2 of the Sixth Schedule:—
“Provided that the Gorkha Hill Council, Darjeeling in the State of West Bengal shall
consist of not more than thirty-three members, of whom twenty-eight shall be elected on the
basis of adult suffrage out of whom ten shall be reserved for the Scheduled Tribes, fifteen
for non-tribal communities, three open for all communities and the remaining five, of which
at least two shall-be women, having same rights including voting rights and privileges as
other members, to be nominated by the Government from amongst the unrepresented
communities of the areas under the Council.”

29
8.7.2 The proposed proviso makes provision for reservation of seats in the proposed Council,
which is in the nature of a local body. The Committee takes note of the fact that the Constitution
(Seventy-third Amendment) Act, 1992 and the Constitution (Seventy-fo urth Amendment) Act, 1992
provide for reservation of not less than one third seats for women in Panchayati Raj institutions
and urban local bodies. This special provision has also been incorporated in the Cantonment
Act, 1924 by a recent amendment. The Committee pointed out that this constitutional reservation
has not been provided in the elected category of the members of the Council.
8.7.3 The Committee accordingly, recommends that thirty three percent reservation for
women should be provided in the composition of the proposed Council. Provision already
exists for reservation of two seats for woman out of five nominated seats. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that nine seats (three out often seats reserved for ST, five out of
fifteen seats reserved for non-tribals and one out of three open seats) should be reserved
for women out of the twenty eight elective seats.
8.7.4 The Committee further noted from the composition of the Council that there is no
provision for reservation for Scheduled Castes. Darjeeling Hill areas have substantial SC
population and there is no reason why reservation to SC should not be provided in the
Council which is a constitutional requirement. The Committee is not convinced by the reply
of the Ministry of Home Affairs that the SC population is not sufficient to provide
reservation to them. The Committee therefore, recommends that necessary reservation to
SCs may be provided in the Council.
8.7.5 The Committee recommends that necessary amendments, may, accordingly be made
in sub-clause (4).
8.7.6 Subject to the above, Clause 2 is adopted.
8.8 Clause 1, Enacting Formula and the Title are adopted with some changes which are
of consequential or drafting nature, namely, “2007” and ‘Fifty-eighth” to be substituted by
“2008” and “Fifty-ninth”, whenever these occur.
8.9 The Committee recommends that the Constitution (One Hundred and Seventh
Amendment) Bill, 2007 and the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution (Amendment) Bill 2007
be passed taking into account amendments suggested in this chapter and the observations
made in Chapter VII.

Secretary of the Ministry made a presentation explaining about the provisions of the Bills.
3.1 The Home Secretary elaborated that these Bills were intended to create an autonomous self
governing council under the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution for the hill areas of Darjeeling
District in the State of West Bengal through constitutional amendments and by transferring 45
subjects of the State Government to the proposed new Gorkha Hill Council. He explained that the
right of non-tribal population, like rights of acquiring land, etc would be protected in the proposed
Council.
4. The Chairperson asked the Home Secretary to explain the reasons for not making provision
for reservation to SCs in the proposed Council despite the Schedule Castes having a population of
one and half lakh. She stated that even the Administrator of DGHC had also demanded for the
reservation to SCs in the proposed council.
5. Responding to the Chairperson’s query, the Home Secretary stated that there was no
provision for reservation to SCs in the present Council and also in the proposed council. He
explained that in the proposed council there were ten seats reserved for Scheduled Tribes, for non-
tribals, three open to all and five seats for nominated category and it had been provided that
unrepresented communities would be given priority in the nominated seats. He informed the
Committee that the SCs constitute 5.7 % of the total population there and through this arrangement,
their representation could be ensured.

37
6. Thereafter, the Chairperson and Members raised the following queries:
(i) The ratio of Tribal population to total population in Darjeeling District.
(ii) The propriety of artificially increasing tribal population to 31.4% by giving tribal status to
'Tamang' and 'Limbus' to create a Tribal Hill Council by amending Sixth Schedule which is
restricted to 'Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Tripura, as there tribals were 12.6% of the
population, according to 2001 Census.
(iii) Need for Legal consultation with Attorney General and other concerned law officers
regarding sustainability of the proposed Bills.
(iv) Comparative analysis of the provisions on executive and financial powers in proposed
Gorkha Hill Council vis-a-vis in other Tribal Councils in other States with Sixth Schedule status.
(v) Studies made by commissions appointed by the Government of India or by the State
Government to assess and confer the ST status to two castes 'Tamang' and 'Limbus' and the
criteria to confer ST status to any group.
(vi) What is the legal status of Shri Subhash Ghising at the time of signing of MOS 2005?
Whether he was drawing salary from the Council or was working as an honorary member? If he
was an employee of the State Government, can a tripartite agreement be legally valid?
(vii) The extent of acceptability of provisions of MOS by the people and their representatives.
(viii) The extent of the legislative powers of the proposed Council.
(ix) Duar sub-Division has not been included in the proposed Council.
(xi) Need for ascertaining views of the Sikkim Government on the proposed Bills as historically,
Darjeeling belongs to the kingdom of Sikkim and Sikkim had given support to Gorkha activities
during the Gorkhaland agitation of 80s.
(xii) The non-Budhists are counted as "Nepali' in Darjeeling.
(xiii) The Demand of Manipur and Arunachal Pradesh for sixth schedule status to certain areas.
7.1 The Members also asked Home Secretary to provide following information to the
Committee.
(i) The report of the survey done by the Cultured Research Institute of India in 2006 on
tribals.
(ii) The names of castes and the break-up of total population among SCs, OBCs and STs
in the Darjeeling Hill Council with reference to 2001 Census.
(iii) The demographic composition of the hill areas of Darjeeling.
(iv) A comparative study of Darjeeling Accord of 1988 and MoS signed in 2005 in a
chart format.
7.2 The representatives of the MHA, assured the Committee to collect and provide the
information sought by it.
8. The Home Secretary in response to the queries raised by the members stated that the
Ministry of Home Affairs had consulted the Ministry of Law and Justice on these Bills. He further
stated that 'Tamangs' and 'Limbus' which have been given tribal status were already listed as STs

38
in Sikkim and the inclusion of these two communities into ST category was not intended to
enhance the tribal population in Darjeeling so as to facilitate to conferment of Sixth schedule status
to it.
9. In response to the queries of members, the Additional Secretary and Registrar General of
India, stated that the ‘Lokur Committee’ set up by the Government of India in 1965 which had
surveyed the whole country and recommended 5 criteria to confer ST status to any group. The
Cabinet Committee on Tribal Affairs had accepted these criteria in 1999 which were slightly
amended in 2002. According to it, any State Government can send a proposal to the Central
Government to confer ST status to a group(s). Then, it is examined by the Registrar General of
India which gives its recommendations. Those are scrutinized by the National Commission for
Scheduled Tribes which in turn gives its report to the Central Government for final decision on
it. ‘Tamng’ and ‘Limbus’ were conferred tribal status through this process.
10. The representative of Ministry of Law and Justice stated that the Sixth Schedule was a self-
contained code for the governance of tribal areas.

6.1.1 Sub-clause (3) of clause 2 provides for insertion of following proviso in paragraph 1,  after

66
6.1.2 Sub-paragraph (2) in paragraph 1 of Sixth Schedule provides that if there are different
Scheduled Tribes in an autonomous district, the Governor may, by public notification, divide the
area inhabited by them into autonomous regions. The Committee noted that by adding the special
proviso, the power of the Governor would be restricted.
6.1.3 The Committee took note of the following clarification given by the Ministry on the
necessity of the proviso and the implications thereof:—
“Sub-paragraph (I) of paragraph 1 of the Sixth Schedule makes provisions about
autonomous districts for tribal areas enumerated in the table appended to paragraph 20 of
the Schedule. Sub-paragraph (2) of paragraph 1 makes provision enabling the Governor to
divide such area or areas into autonomous regions if there are different Scheduled Tribes
in an autonomous district. Sub-paragraph (I) of paragraph 2 makes provision for the
composition of District Councils in terms of the total number of elected and nominated
members.
These provisions have remained unaltered with reference to Autonomous Hill Councils
in respect of various areas which have been constituted under the Sixth Schedule to the
Constitution from time to time. However in the case of the Bodoland Territorial Council,
the following two distinctive pr ovisions were made:—
(i) a provision was made whereby nothing in sub-paragraph (2) of paragraph 1 would
apply to the Bodoland Territorial Areas District; and
(ii) specific provision was made in sub-paragraph (1) of paragraph 2 through a
proviso indicating the composition of the Council which was different from the
general composition stipulated in sub-paragraph (I) of paragraph 1.
These changes were necessitated on account of the fact that the decision to include
the areas of Bodoland Territorial Areas District had been arrived at as a part of an Accord
in which, inter alia, the specific territories to be covered and the composition of the
Council were also decided.
In the case of the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council also the proposal to bring it under
the Sixth Schedule follows Tripartite discussions between Government of India, Government
of West Bengal and Shri Subash Ghisingh (President, GNLF and Administrator, DGHC) and
a Memorandum of Settlement in which specific provisions were made pertaining to the area
to be brought under the Council (which was part of the District of Darjeeling) and the
composition of the Council. Keeping this in view similar provisions as in the case of the
Bodoland Territorial Council have been made with reference to non-application of sub-
paragraph (2) of paragraph 1 of the Sixth Schedule.
The underlying logic is that where, on the basis of an Accord or Settlement specific
provisions regarding the area and composition of the Council have been made in the
Constitution, the existing provision in sub-paragraph (2) of paragraph 1 enabling the
Governor to divide such area or areas into autonomous regions would no longer be required”.
In view of the above clarification of the Ministry, the Committee adopted sub-clause (3)
without any change.
6.1.4 The Committee then took up sub-clause (4) of clause 2, which seeks to insert following
proviso after sub-paragraph (1) in paragraph 2 ofthe Sixth Schedule:—
“Provided that the Gorkha Hill Council, Darjeeling in the State of West Bengal shall
consist of not more than thirty-three members, of whom twenty-eight shall be elected on

67
the basis of adult suffrage out of whom ten shall be reserved for the Scheduled Tribes,
fifteen for non-tribal communities, three open for all communities and the remaining five,
of which at least two shall be women, having same rights including voting rights and
privileges as other members, to be nominated by the Government from amongst the
unrepresented communities of the areas under the Council.”
6.1.5 The proposed proviso makes provision for reservation of seats in the proposed Council,
which is in the nature of a local body. The Committee took note of the fact that the Constitution
(Seventy-third Amendment) Act, 1992 and the Constitution (Seventy-fourth Amendment) Act, 1992
provide for reservation of not less than one third seats for women in Panchayati Raj institutions
and urban local bodies. This special provision had also been incorporated in the Cantonment
Act, 1924 by a recent amendment. The Committee felt that this constitutional reservation had not
been provided in the elected category of the members of the Council.
6.1.6 The Committee, accordingly, felt that thirty three per cent reservation for women should be
provided in the composition of the proposed Council. Provision already exists for reservation of
two seats for woman out of five nominated seats. The Committee, felt that nine seats (three out
of ten seats reserved for ST, five out of fifteen seats reserved for non-tribals and one out of three
open seats) should be reserved for women, out of the twenty eight elective seats.
6.1.7 The Committee further noted from the composition of the Council that there was no
provision for reservation for Scheduled Castes. The Committee was of the view that Darjeeling Hill
areas had substantial SC population and there was no reason why reservation to SC should not be
provided in the Council which is a constitutional requirement. The Committee was not convinced
by the reply of the Ministry of Home Affairs that the SC population was not sufficient to provide
reservation to them and felt that necessary reservation to SC should be provided in the Council.
The Committee recommended that necessary amendments, may, accordingly be made in sub-
clause (4).
6.1.8 Subject to the above, Clause 2 was adopted.
Enacting Formula and the Title

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
The provisions of the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution have evolved a
separate scheme for the administration of the tribal areas in the S tates of Assam,
Meghalaya, Mizoram and Tripura through the District Councils or Regional
Councils. The provisions in paragraphs 1 to 17 of the said Sixth Schedule relate
to the administration of the autonomous areas under that Schedule. The Councils
are vested with legislative powers on specified subjects and are allotted certain
sources of taxation. They have also been given powers to set up and administer
their system of justice and maintain administrative and welfare services in
respect of land, revenue, forests, education, public health etc. So far, the
application of the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution has not been extended to
any other State of the Union, besides North-Eastern States.
2. Two Memoranda of Settlement (came to be known as ‘Darjeeling
Accord’) signed between the Government of India, Government of West Bengal
and the Gorkha National Liberation Front (GNLF) on 22-23 August, 1988 had
put an end to the violent agitation launched by the GNLF primarily demanding
creation of a separate State of Gorkhaland, and paved the way for fulfillment of
socio-economic and political aspirations of the hill people of Darjeeling district.
An autonomous hill council, viz., Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council (DGHC) was set
up through the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council Act, 1988 enacted by the
Government of West Bengal on 15.10.1988, with full executive control on
certain subjects. The DGHC has a council of 42 members with 28 elected and
14 nominated members and with a term of five years.
3. The Darjeeling Accord however, could not fulfill the aspirations of the
hill people of Darjeeling and GNLF has been agitating for the past few years for
conferring constitutional status on the Nepali dominated areas in the Darjeeling
hill areas. A number of tripartite meetings between Government of India,
Government of West Bengal and GNLF were held to resolve the issues and it
emerged that the only solution lies in according Sixth Schedule status to certain
areas of Darjeeling District within the State of West Bengal under exceptional
circumstances as was done in the case of Bodo land Territorial Council (BTC)
within the State of Assam. An exception was made for BTC and the area was
accorded Sixth Schedule status even though the members of the Scheduled Tribe
communities (STs) were not in majority and reportedly comprised only 38 per
cent of the population of the area. However, certain safeguards for the Non-
Tribals residing in the BTC areas were provided and the Sixth Schedule to the
Constitution was accordingly amended. As per the sample check carried out
during 22-26 October, 2005 by the Registrar-General of India, the total ST
population constituted about 31.4 per cent of the total population of existing
DGHC areas.
4. An ‘In Principle’ Memorandum of Settlement (MOS) was signed on
06.12.2005 between the Government of India, Government of West Bengal and
Administrator, Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council (DGHC) for creating an
autonomous self governing Council under the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution
79

80
for the hill areas of Darjeeling District within the State of West Bengal following
due consultative, legislative and constitutional processes by the State and Central
Governments, so as to fulfil the economic, educational and linguistic aspirations,
socio-cultural and ethnic identity of the hill people, duly protecting the rights of
the non-tribals, and to speed up the infrastructure development in the hill areas
of Darjeeling District. In terms of the MOS, the existing DGHC will be replaced
by an autonomous self governing Council called Gorkha Hill Council, Darjeeling
(GHC) in the State of West Bengal under the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution.
The State Government, at an appropriate time, will dissolve the DGHC and repeal
the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council Act, 1988 to pave the way for creation of
GHC.
5. With a view to meet the aspirations of the people of the hill areas of
Darjeeling District and in pursuance of the MOS dated 06.12.2005, it is proposed
to—
(i) create an autonomous self governing Council called the Gorkha
Hill Council, Darjeeling (GHC) under the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution
within the State of West Bengal, which shall have legislative, administrative
and financial powers in respect of specified subjects; and
(ii) provide for adequate safeguards for the non-tribals to ensure that
any law as may be made by the GHC will not, in particular:—
(a) extinguish or modify the existing rights and privileges
enjoyed by any citizen including his land rights within the areas under
the GHC at the commencement of the Sixth Schedule to the
Constitution (Amendment) Act, 2007; and
(b) bar any citizen from acquiring land either by way of
inheritance, allotment, settlement or by way of transfer if such citizen
is otherwise eligible for such bona fide  acquisition of land within the
areas under GHC.
6. The Bill seeks to achieve the aforesaid objectives.

6. In its background note supplied to the Committee the Ministry of. Law, Justice 
and Company Affairs explained the necessity for amending section 28 of the Indian 
Contract Act, 1872 as under :-
(i) The Law Commission of India has recommended, in its 97th Repon, 
amendment in section 28 of the Indian Contract Act. 1872. The subject 
was taken up by the Law Commission on its own having regard to its 
imponan ce and relevance. The Report addresses itself to an anomalous 
situation that prevails under the present law in regard to prescriptive 
clauses in contracts. Such clauses .tim at extinguishing rights under a 
contraCt on the expiry of a specified period. The subject is of great 
importance from the point of view of economic justice, avoidance of 
hardship to consumers and symm etry of the law. 
(ii) Under section 28 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, an agreement which 
limits the time within which a party to an agreement may enforce his 
rights in a court is void to that extent. But the Section does not 
invalidate an agreement which provides that if the rights are not enforced 
at the end of a specified period, such rights shall cease to exist. lt may 
be stated that such stipulatio ns are frequently found in agreements entered 
into in the course of business. 
(iii) The relevant part of section 28 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 reads as 
under 
"Every agreement, by which any party thereto is restricted 
absolutely from enforcing his rights under or in respect of any 
contract by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary tribunals, 
or which limits the time within which he may thus enforce his 
rights, is void to that extent." 
\ 
(iv) In such a case, which went upto the Supreme Court, a clause in an 
insurance policy provided that all benefits under the insurance policy shall 
be forfeited if a suit was not brought within a specified period. The 
clause was held to be valid (AIR 1976 SC 287). This judgement 
expressly approved the decisions of the High Courts taking a similar view 
(AIR 1914 Born 223, AIR 1924 Cal. 186 and AIR 1974 Bom. 228). 
These cases hold that it is only when a period of limitation is curtailed 
that section 28 of the Contract Act comes into operation. As was 
observed in a Bombay case, 'lf (Section 28) does not come into 
operation when the (contractu al) term spells ou t an extinction of the right

PREFACE
I, the Chairperson of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home
Affairs, having been authorized by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby
present this One Hundred and Thirtieth Report on Action Taken by the Government on the
Recommendations/Observations contained in the One Hundred and Twenty Sixth Report on
Demands for Grants (2007-08) of the Ministry of Home Affairs.
2. The One Hundred and Twenty Sixth Report of the Department-related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Home Affairs was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok
Sabha on 26th April, 2007.
3. The Ministry of Home Affairs furnished the Action Taken Replies on the One Hundred and
Twenty Sixth Report of the Committee on 18th September, 2007. The Minister for Home Affairs
made a Statement in the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha on the status of implementation of
recommendations contained in the said report of the Committee on 4th and 5th December, 2007,
respectively pursuant to the Direction of the Chairman, Rajya Sabha dated 24th September, 2004.
4. The Committee considered the draft Report and adopted the same at its meeting held on
11th April, 2008.
5. The Recommendations/Observations of the Committee are printed in bold letters.
SUSHMA SWARAJ
N
EW D ELHI; Chairperson,
11th April, 2008 Department-related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Home Affairs

1
REPORT
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the Ministry
of Home Affairs on the recommendations contained in the One Hundred Twenty Sixth Report
(of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs) on Demands for
Grants for 2007-08. The Report was presented/laid on the Table of Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha
on the 26th April, 2007.
2. Action Taken Notes have been received from the Ministry of Home Affairs in respect of
the recommendations contained in the Report. Subsequently, the Minister for Home Affairs laid on
the Table of Lok Sabha/Rajya Sabha a statement on the status of implementation of
recommendations contained in that report. Those have been categorized as follows:
(i) Chapter—I: Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the
Government: Para Nos. 8.7, 14.5, 15.6, 15.7, 15.10, 15.11 & 15.12, 16.5, 16.6, 18.1,
19.3, 20.18, 21.9 and 24.5.
2.1 The Committee is pleased to observe that the Ministry has accepted all its recommendations
as contained in Chapter—I of the Report.
(ii) Chapter—II: Recommendations/Observations on which the Committee does not desire
to pursue the matter in view of the Government’s replies: Para Nos. 11.10,
14.6, 21.7, 21.8, 24.3 & 24.4.
(iii) Chapter—III: Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the
Government have not been accepted by the Committee: Para Nos. 9.2, 10.4, 11.8,
11.11, 13.9, 14.8, 17.8 & 24.6.
2.2 The Committee expresses its concern over the non-implementation of recommendations
contained in Chapter—III and desires that the Ministry should furnish logical explanation in respect
of these recommendations.
(iv) Chapter—IV: Recommendations/Observations in respect of which the final replies of
the Government have not yet been received by the Committee: Para Nos 11.7, 12.3,
13.7, 16.7, 17.3, 17.7, 20.19 and 23.6.
2.3 In respect of recommendations placed in Chapter—IV , the Ministry has either furnished
the interim replies or couched its response in vague terms. The Committee, therefore, desires that
the Ministry should furnish Action Taken Notes in respect of recommendations categorized in
Chapter—IV in detail and to the point as per the intention and spirit of the recommendations of
the Committee.
3. The details of the ATNs have been discussed in the various Chapters of the Report.

2
CHAPTER–I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS WHICH
HA VE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
Recommendation
1.1 Civic Action Programme of Border Guarding Forces
1.1.1 The Committee feels that Civic Action Programme in the border areas is a very important
task. If undertaken well, it will infuse confidence among the border area populace, develop
infrastructure there and promote the feeling of national integration. For all these to happen, the
people should have confidence in the persons who are undertaking such activities. However, people
are skeptical about the uniformed personnel. The Committee therefore recommends that the
implementation of Civic Action Programme by the BGFs need to be re-looked in its entirety.
(Para 8.7)
Action Taken
1.1.2 The C ivic Action Programme was thoroughly discussed, in a meeting held on 25.5.2007
under the Chairmanship of Home Secretary with Border Guarding Forces.
1.1.3 The DGs were unanimous in their opinion that the Civic Action Programme has enabled the
CPFs to win the goodwill of the border population and has had a very positive impact. Therefore
the programme should continue with higher fund allocation. Accordingly, the allocation for Civic
Action Programme undertaken by CPFs has been enhanced substantially in the current financial year.
1.1.4 During the review of the programme, apart from the type of activities taken up at present
under the programme, it was also decided that CPFs could usefully act as a facilitator for better
delivery of various important Government Schemes in the far flung areas of the country where
practically only they have the reach. Towards this objective, consultation with various Ministries
is in progress. Some joint programmes with Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports have already been
worked out.
Committee’s Observation
1.1.5 The Committee notes that allocation for Civic Action Programme has been enhanced.
The activities proposed to be taken, if implemented in the right earnest, would go a long
way in infusing a sense of confidence in the people of border areas.
Recommendation
1.2 Naxalism
1.2.1 The Committee notes that the Government is taking steps on different fronts including the
developmental fronts. The Committee has also recommended in successive reports for a holistic
approach in tackling the naxal problem. The Committee however, feels that there is no perceptible
change on the socio-economic front. Though the socio-economic development cannot be quantified,
it can be perceived and if such a perceptible change is there, undoubtedly it will have a lasting
impact. The Committee while reiterating the earlier recommendation that an effective developmental
approach may be adopted, further recommends that various schemes under the Ministries of Rural
Development and other Ministries may also be implemented for the socio-economic development in
2

3
the naxal affected areas. There needs to be an effective monitoring mechanism on the
implementation of these schemes with the involvement of all the concerned Ministries and agencies.
(Para 14.5)
Action Taken
1.2.2 The Ministry agrees with the recommendation of the Committee that a holistic approach,
comprising both the security and developmental aspects is required to tackle the naxal problem. The
Central Government is supplementing the efforts and resources of the State Governments on both
these fronts. The aim is that development schemes, both of the Central Government and of the
concerned State Governments, are effectively implemented.
1.2.3 An Inter Ministerial Group (IMG) has been set up under Additional Secretary (Naxal
Management) with officers from development Ministries/Departments (including Rural
Development) and Planning Commission to oversee effective implementation of development
schemes in naxal affected States. This is intended to ensure accelerated socio-economic
development in these areas by improving overall implementation of development schemes.
1.2.4 Union Home Secretary inter alia also reviews development issues of naxal affected States
in quarterly meetings of Coordination Centre in which the concerned State Governments are
represented by Chief Secretaries and Directors General of Police. Inter-Ministerial discussions are
also proposed at the level of Union Home Secretary with Ministries of Rural Development,
Panchayati Raj, Environment and Forests and Tribal Affairs in order to work out a methodology
for more focussed action in respect of the implementation of development schemes in the States
affected by naxal activities.
1.2.5 An Empowered Group of Ministers (EGoM) has also been constituted under the
Chairmanship of Union Home Minister, which includes the Union Ministers of concerned
development Ministries like Rural Development, Tribal Welfare and Panchayati Raj and is
empowered to determine and monitor various aspects of the integrated strategy required to be
followed to deal with the naxalite problem.
Recommendation
1.3 Modernisation of Police Forces
1.3.1 The Committee takes note of the Mid-Term evaluation of the Modernisation of State Police
Forces Scheme by BPR&D. One of the findings made by the BPR&D in the Study which causes
concern to the Committee is that more than 50 per cent of the fund is utilized in the police housing
and police building activities. The Committee is of the view that with the new technological
advances taking place in a feverish pitch and in view of the fact that the Police Forces in India
function with age-old equipments and gadgets, much of the scheme of modernization should
concentrate on providing modern gadgets, improving technology, providing IT facilities etc.
Spending more than 50 per cent on building activities defeats the very purpose of the Scheme. The
Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs may review the
scheme in the light of pattern of expenditure incurred by the States and prepare a list of activities
which should lay thrust on improving technology and providing modern gadgets, etc.
(Para 15.6)
Action Taken
1.3.2 The concerns expressed by the Committee regarding large amount of funds being utilized
for police housing and police building activities and the need for giving mere emphasis on induction
of modern technology is appreciated and duly noted. Accordingly, in the meetings held in the
Ministry for considering the Annual Action Plans, under the Scheme for Modernisation of State

4
Police Forces (MPF) for the year 2007-08, the State Gevernments were advised to rationalize the
allocation on police housing, etc., and to lay greater emphasis on other aspects of police
modernization such as procurement of modern gadgetry, sophisticated equipments/weaponry etc.
1.3.3 In this regard, it may be noted that the Annual Action Plans under the Scheme for
Modernisation of State Police Forces (MPF) are formulated by the State Governments after
assessing their urgent local requirements. These plans are discussed in the meetings held by the
Central Level High Powered Committee, which are attended by the State representatives also. All
critical items like construction of residential/non-residential buildings, modern weaponry, vehicles,
communication equipment, office equipment, surveillance/intelligence/security equipments, training
facilities, forensic science equipment etc. are covered under the Scheme. Construction of police
station buildings and residential buildings (barracks) for lower subordinates are major components
of the scheme. These are also considered essential as they enhance the morale of the State Police
Forces and are therefore, directly concerned with their efficiency. The improvement in police
performance due to modernization, to a considerable extent, will also depend on the provision of
the basic necessary infrastructure in all the police stations as well as in the district police
headquarters.
1.3.4 Emphasis is also being laid on providing IT facilities. A Project called “Common Integrated
Police Application” (CIPA) is being implemented in all the States to ensure a uniform framework
and mechanism for computerization of the crime registration, investigation, etc. at the police station
level. NIC is the implementing agency for the project, which is being implemented in all the States
in a phased manner.
1.3.5 The Ministry is now planning major thrust on technology upgradation in the functioning of
police at all levels. This is proposed to be done by widening the scope of the CIPA project in terms
of the applications and by extending it from the police stations to the other higher level formations
in the police hierarchy e.g. the circle/districts/range/zonal offices and the police headquarters, for
consolidating the police station databases at a central location and providing appropriate software
interfaces for interaction and sharing of crime related information. At present, CIPA essentially has
crime registration, investigation and prosecution modules. It is now proposed to provide all
functionalities and integrate appropriate technologies, such as, fingerprinting and other forensic
science applications in a large network, so that the information and technology can be shared by
all concerned. For this purpose, the police stations and other higher police formations are also
proposed to be linked through a broadband/CDMA/VSAT network. A comprehensive composite
proposal has been sent to the Planning Commission for including the project under the Eleventh
Five Year Plan (2007-12). When accepted, larger share of funds shall become available within the
Modernisation of Police Forces (non-plan Scheme) for spending on the other essential requirements
like modem weaponry, equipment, construction of secure police stations, etc.
Further Recommendation
1.3.6 The Committee notes that the Ministry of Home Affairs has forwarded the
“Comprehensive Composite Proposal” to the Planning Commission for technology
upgradation in the functioning of police at all level through a pr oject called CIPA—crime
registration, investigation, and prosecution modules to be linked through a broadband/
CDMA/VSAT network. The Committee desires that the Planning Commission may clear the
project at the earliest.
Recommendation
1.4 Modernisation of Police Forces
1.4.1 The Committee is constrained to note that there wa s an unspent balance of Rs.47.81 crore

5
under the Scheme of Modernisation of Police Forces as on 31.12.2006. Though the Ministry have
stated that they are pursuing vigorously with the States for better and full utilization of funds, the
Committee desires that they may lay a condition stating that further funds would be released only
after the full expenditure of the previous balance. It should be insisted upon all the States to send
Utilization Certificates and receipt thereof may also be put as one of the conditions for further
release of funds. These are necessary to ensure that States spend the funds meant for
Modernization of Police Forces in a better manner and as per the schedule.
(Para 15.7)
Action Taken
1.4.2 The Government is in full agreement with the recommendation. The importance and

2.1 National Disaster Management Authority

Action Taken
2.1.2 Department of Ocean Development (DOD), Ministry of Earth Sciences is setting up

INCOIS,V-SAT Communication at INCOIS Hyderabad, for receiving real time data from National
Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT), has been established and at present real-time data is being
received at INCOIS through V-SAT Connectivity from tide gauges and Bottom Pressure Recorders.
2.1.4 As against total budget outlay of this project i.e. Rs.125 crore, Rs.87 crore have already
been spent and the system is scheduled to be operational by September, 2007.
Recommendation
2.2 Naxalism
2.2.1 The Committee also reiterates its observation made earlier that the naxal problem is no
longer a problem of a few States. It has acquired a national dimension posing gravest threat to the
national security. The naxal activities have spread to more than twelve States and are reported to
be having links with external agencies including ISI. The Committee is therefore, of the considered
view that taking into account the growth and influence of the Naxal groups in several States and
the grave threat posed by it to the internal security of the country, it is high time that the Ministry
constitute a Unified Command to effectively tackle the menace. Besides the Central Paramilitary
Forces, State Police Forces may also contribute to the Unified Command. The Committee also
takes note of the observation made by the Home Secretary that naxal attacks on several occasions
take place due to non-observance of ‘Standard Operating Procedure’ (SOP) by the State Police
13

14
Forces. The Committee therefore, strongly recommends that Government may consider creating a
Unified Command common to all the naxal affected States.
(Para 14.6)
Action Taken
2.2.2 Law and Order is a State subject. The Central Government is supplementing the efforts and
resources of the State Governments through a variety of measures, including deployment of Central
Para Military Forces which work under the command of the concerned State Governments,
strengthening of the local Police and Intelligence agencies through the Scheme for Modernisation
of State Police Forces, provision of financial assistance through the Scheme of Security Related
Expenditure, sharing of Intelligence and bringing about inter-State coordination.
1.2.3 For review, coordination and evaluation of the naxalite situation, among other institutional
mechanisms like an Empowered Group of Ministers under the chairmanship of Union Home
Minister with Chief Ministers of concerned States as special invitees and a Coordination Centre
under the Chairmanship of Union Home Secretary, a Task Force under Special Secretary (Internal
Security), consisting of officers of Intelligence agencies, Central Para Military Forces and
concerned State Police Forces, has also been set up to deliberate upon the various steps needed
to deal with the activities of naxalites and to bring about co-ordination between authorities of
different States as may be necessary.
1.2.4 The system of a Unified Command can be implemented within a particular State, as has
been done in some States affected by violence (for example, Jammu and Kashmir) with the
objective of ensuring coordination between State and Central agencies involved in internal security
duties within the State. Any such mechanism. is not constitutionally or otherwise feasible with
reference to multiple States being brought under any kind of a unified command. However, the
need for inter-State coordination has been fully recognized, and that is the reason for setting up
of the Task Force referred to above. It is constantly the endeavour that this mechanism functions
in the most effective manner and, towards that end, the Task Force has also been having
discussions and interactions with different groups of States with reference to the specific inter-
State coordination requirements in different areas from time to time.

Action Taken
3.8.2 To enable the shooters to excel in international events, the Government has already allowed

23
“Renowned Shooters” to import the advanced weapons ( i.e. four per event subject to a maximum
of ten).
3.8.3 W ith a view to enable a larger number of shooters to have an opportunity to import
sophisticated weapons for practice at private ranges etc. and to come upto international level of
shooting sports, the Government has decided to enlarge the definition of “Renowned Shooter” as
follows :—
“Renowned Shooter” means a person who has participated in a National Shooting
Championship in an open Men’ s Event or open Women’ s Event or open Civilian’s Event

Qualifying Score prescribed by the National Rifle Association of India.’’

Further Recommendation
3.8.5 It has been brought to the notice of the Committee by one of its member that the
following conditions imposed by the Ministry make disposal of weapons by renowned shooter
difficult:—
(a) Before allowing disposal of weapons by the renowned shooters, the condition of
the weapons may be assessed by a 3-member committee proposed to be
constituted under the Chairmanship of the Executive Director (Teams), Sports
Authority of India, with a representative each from NRAI and the National
Coach of Shooting as other members and disposal will be allowed only on the
recommendation of this committee.
(b) While disposing of such weapons, it would be ensured that these are being sold
to other upcoming shooters only subject to production of certificate to this effect
from the concerned State Association. A promising shooter would be one who
would have finished among the first three in the preceding State level
championships. After disposal, intimation to this effect will be given by the
renowned shooter to the NRAI, the Sports Authority of India and the Ministry
of Youth Affairs and Sports.
3.8.6 The Ministry, however, did not bring the above conditions to the notice of the
Committee.
3.8.7 The Committee is of the considered view that the above mentioned conditions would
create problems in the smooth disposal of outdated weapons by renowned shooters. The
meeting of the three member committee to decide disposal of weapons may not be held for
months together and the players would have no option but to wait for the outcome of the
decision of the Committee which may affect his practice/profession. Moreover, fulfilling the
condition of disposal of weapons only to promising shooters who have finished among the
first three in the preceding State level championship, would be a herculean task for the
seller shooter. The shooters who finished first three may no longer be interested in buying
outdated weapons. The Committee therefore recommends that Government may remove the
conditions of the endorsement by the three member Committee and instead straightway
allow sale of weapon by a renowned shooter to any shooter registered with Rifle Clubs/
District/State/National Rifle Association.

4.6.7 The Committee has appointed a sub-committee to make a detailed study of Housing
Schemes for Delhi Police Personnel and Central Police Forces. After the study is complete,
the Committee will present a separate report thereon.
Recommendation
4.7 Demand No.94 – Andaman and Nicobar Islands
4.7.1 The Committee also understands that the Island Administration has a proposal of

29
procurement of two fixed wing aircrafts and two helicopters which is held up in Ministry of Civil
Aviation. The Ministry of Civil Aviation may clear the proposal at the earliest. The Ministry of
Home Affairs may also consult the Ministry of Civil Aviation for an early clearance of the proposal.
(Para 20.19)
Action Taken
4.7.2 Ministry of Civil Aviation has completed the Techno-Economic Evaluation of the proposal
and M/s Pawan Hans Helicopters Ltd. has been authorized to procure two 11-15 seaters helicopters
and two fixed wing aircrafts (one each of 9-10 seater and 15-19 seater) on behalf of A&N
Administration. M/s Pawan Hans Helicopters Ltd. has finalized EFC Memo for procurement of fixed
wing aircraft and the same has been sent to UT Administration for vetting. EFC Memo for
helicopters is still under preparation.
Further Recommendation
4.7.3 The Committee would like to be informed of the final outcome of the efforts made.
Recommendation
4.8 Demand No. 96–Dadra and Nagar Haveli; and
Demand No. 97–Daman and Diu
4.8.1 The Committee is constrained to note that both the Union Territories of Daman and Diu and
Dadra and Nagar Haveli have been getting very less grant as compared to the projections made by
them. In fact, Dadra and Nagar Haveli has been given about one-third of the projected amount
whereas Daman and Diu has been less than 50 per cent of the projected amount. With this
reduction in the allocations, the activities proposed to be taken up by the Union Territories would
be considerably affected. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the allocations for
both the Union Territories may be increased appropriately at RE level. The Ministry of Home Affairs
may also hold discussions with the Planning Commission about the necessity of the projects to be
taken up by the Union Territories. The Committee also recommends that the priority areas of
activities proposed to be taken up during 2007-08 may be completed as per the targets fixed.
Energy sector is an important area in which both the Union Territories proposed to set up new
sub-stations. Dadra and Nagar Haveli also proposed to augment the capacity of a sub-station and
Daman and Diu proposes to convert overhead lines to underground lines. These activities may be
undertaken on a priority basis and completed as per the targets fixed.
(Para 23.6)
Action Taken replies
4.8.2 The Union Territory Administration of Daman and Diu and Dadra and Nagar Haveli have
taken up the matter with the Planning Commission to augment the Plan allocation to Rs.190 crore
and Rs.232 crore, respectively, at RE 2007-08 stage. Ministry of Home Affairs has also requested
Planning Commission in July, 2007 to consider the proposal of these UTs favourably. MHA has also
taken up with Planning Commission for revival of the practice of consultation/discussions with the
two UT Adminsitrations for finalizing their Annual Plan Outlays. Planning Commission has agreed
to revive the practice from next Annual Plan.
4.8.3 Necessary actions are being expedited to complete activities proposed to be taken up during
2007-08 as per the targets fixed.
Further Recommendation
4.8.4 The Committee would like to be informed the present status of various activities
taken up in 2007-08 along with the targets and achievements.

AT A GLANCE
Civic Action Programme of Border Guarding Forces
The Committee notes that allocation for Civic Aviation Programme has been
enhanced. The activities proposed to be taken, if implemented in the right earnest, would
go a long way in infusing a sense of confidence in the people of border areas.
(Para 1.1.5)
1.3 Modernisation of Police Forces
The Committee notes that the Ministry of Home Affairs has forwarded the
"Comprehensive Composite Proposal" to the Planning Commission for technology
upgradation in the functioning of police at all level through a project called CIP A-crime
registration, investigation, and prosecution modules to be linked through a broadband/
CDMA/VSAT network. The Committee desires that the Planning Commission may clear the

The Committee has appointed a sub-Committee to make a detailed study of the
scheme. After the study is completed by the sub-Committee a separate and detailed report

Recommendation

Relief and rehabilitation measures for J&K migrants
The Committee has appointed a sub-Committee to make a detailed study on the

Coastal Security Scheme
The Committee is constrained to note that even though the scheme was approved in

31
National Disaster Management Authority
The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs should expediously
consider the Draft National Policy on Disaster Management as prepared by the National
Disaster Management Authority and finalize the policy at the earliest. The country can not
wait for a disaster to happen before the policy is finalized. (Para 3.3.3)
National Disaster Management Authority
It is unfortunate that the constitution of NDRF is still at consultation stage. The
Government should take early action in the matter and see that NDRF is in place
converging CRF/NCCF. (Para 3.4.6)
The Committee notes that a provision for creation of National Disaster Mitigation
Fund was made way lack in DM Act, 2005. Undue delay has taken place in discussion of
MHA with the Ministry of Finance, the National Disaster Management Authority and
Planning Commission. The Committee recommends that the process of creating the fund
may be completed at the earliest. (Para 3.4.7)
India-Bangladesh Border Fencing Work
The Committee has constituted a sub-Committee to make a detailed study of the
Border fencing and Floodlighting projects. After the study is completed, the Committee will
present a separate report thereon. (Para 3.5.5)
Naxalism
Naxalism is no longer the problem of one State. As part of holistic approach, the
private sector also needs to be protected. The economic development of naxal affected areas
can happen only if private sector also contributes to this. Therefore, there is need for
making a policy for protecting industries including private sector. (Para 3.6.5)
Housing for Delhi Police Personnel
The Committee was appointed a sub-Committee to make a detailed study of the
Housing for CPMF and Delhi Police. After the study is completed by the sub-Committee, the
Committee will present its detailed report thereon. (Para 3.7.5)
Acquiring of weapons by sportspersons
It has been brought to the notice of the Committee by one of its member that the
following conditions imposed by the Ministry make disposal of weapons by renowned shooter
difficult:—
(a) Before allowing disposal of weapons by the renowned shooters, the condition of
the weapons may be assessed by a 3-member committee proposed to be
constituted under the Chairmanship of the Executive Director (Teams), Sports
Authority of India, with a representative each from NRAI and the National
Coach of Shooting as other members and disposal will be allowed only on the
recommendation of this committee.
(b) While disposing of such weapons, it would be ensured that these are being sold
to other upcoming shooters only subject to production of certificate to this effect
from the concerned State Association. A promising shooter would be one who
would have finished among the first three in the preceding State level
championships. After disposal, intimation to this effect will be given by the
renowned shooter to the NRAI, the Sports Authority of India and the Ministry
of Youth Affairs and Sports. (Para 3.8.5)

32
The Ministry, however, did not bring the above conditions to the notice of the
Committee. (Para 3.8.6)
The Committee is of the considered view that the above mentioned conditions would
create problems in the smooth disposal of outdated weapons by renowned shooters. The
meeting of the three member committee to decide disposal of weapons may not be held for
months together and the players would have no option but to wait for the outcome of the
decision of the committee which may affect his practice/profession. Moreover, fulfilling the
condition of disposal of weapons only to promising shooters who have finished among the
first three in the preceding State level championship, would be a herculean task for the
seller shooter. The shooters who finished first three may no longer be interested in buying
outdated weapons. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Government may remove
the conditions of the endorsement by the three member committee and instead straightway
allow sale of weapon by a renowned shooter to any shooter registered with Rifle Clubs/
District/State/National Rifle Association. (Para 3.8.7)
