PREFACE
I, the Chairperson of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home
Affairs, having been authorized by the Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby
present this One Hundred and Forty First Report on the Action Taken by Government on the
recommendations/observations contained in its One Hundred and Thirty-third Report on Demands
for Grants (2008-09) of the Ministry of Development of North-Eastern Region.
2. The One Hundred and Thirty-third Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Home Affairs was presented to the Parliament on 16 April, 2008.
3. The Ministry of Development of North-Eastern Region (DoNER) furnished the Action Taken
Note on the One Hundred and Thirty-third Report of the Committee on 13th August, 2008.
4. The Committee considered the draft Report and adopted the same at its meeting held on
24th February, 2009.
5. Recommendations/Observations of the Committee are printed in bold letters.
SUSHMA SWARAJ
N
EW D ELHI; Chairperson,
24 February, 2009 Department-related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Home Affairs.

1
REPORT
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the Ministry of
Development of North Eastern Region on the recommendations contained in the One Hundred
and Thirty-third Report of the Committee on Demands for Grants (2008-09). The One Hundred
Thirty-third Report was presented to/laid on the Table of Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha on the
16 April, 2008.
2. Action Taken Notes as received from the Ministry of DoNER in respect of the
recommendations contained in the Report, have been categorized as follows:
Chapter–I: The recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the
Government: Paras: 7.5; 7.6; 8.6; 8.13; 8.14; 9.10; 10.9; 13.8; 15.9, 15.10;
16.10; 16.12; 18.8; 19.4; 20.3; 21.7 (of the One Hundred and Thirty-third Report).
The Committee is happy to note that the Ministry has accepted its recommendation as
mentioned in Chapter–I of the Report.
Chapter–II: The recommendations/observations in respect of which the Committee
has not accepted or is not satisfied with the replies of the Ministry: Paras: 11.7;
12.10; 16.11; 16.13; 21.6; 22.5 (
ibid).
The Committee expresses its concern over the non-implementation or unsatisfactory
implementation of recommendations contained in Chapter-II and desires that the Ministry should
furnish logical explanation and convincing responses in respect of those recommendations.
Chapter–III: The recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of
the Government have not been received: paras 14.4; 15.11; 17.4 (
ibid).
The Ministry has furnished either incomplete or interim replies in respect of
recommendations placed in Chapter–III. Therefore, the Committee desires that the Ministry should
furnish Action Taken Notes in respect of the recommendations categorized in Chapter–III detailed
and pointed in the light of the letter and spirit of the recommendations of the Committee.
3. The details of the A TNs have been discussed in various Chapters in the succeeding pages.

2
CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED
BY THE GOVERNMENT
1.1 OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF THE DEMANDS FOR GRANTS
Recommendation
1.1.1 The Committee is concerned that even though the Ministry of DoNER made a projection of
Rs.2922 crore for the current year, the actual allocation made was Rs.1455 crore under plan
scheme. The Committee has been given to understand that due to the reduction in the allocation
by almost 50%, many projects would suffer. The Ministry will not be able to implement the schemes
for the development of the region. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the
allocation to the Ministry be made as per its requirement as it would be in the interest of the
overall development of the North-East Region. (Para 7.5 of 133rd Report)
Action Taken
1.1.2 The Ministry of DoNER had sought allocations of Rs. 1200 crore each under the NEC and
NLCPR Plan Schemes. These are major Plan Schemes of the Ministry for 2008-09. However,
Planning Commission allocated Rs. 624 crore and Rs.650 crore respectively for the said Schemes
for 2008-09.
1.1.3 Immediately after the allocation of BE 2008-09 provision for NEC and NLCPR Plan
Schemes, the Ministry of DoNER has taken up the issue of higher allocation with the Planning
Commission. Discussions are presently going on at the highest level.
Further Recommendation
1.1.4 The Committee reiterates its recommendation that the Planning Commission should
consider making budgetary allocation to the Ministry of DoNER as per its requirement, so
that the projects undertaken should not remain incomplete for want of funds.
1.2 OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF THE DEMANDS FOR GRANTS
Recommendation
1.2.1 The Committee is not convinced by the reasoning given by the Secretary, NEC on the
visibility aspect of the development. The component of private investment is a totally different
matter to be viewed in the proper context and perspective. First of all, the outcome of the public
investments should be visible and transparent. Then only a positive message will go for private
investment. The Committee appreciates that there are basic and inherent problems in converting
public investment into tangible results. That can only be achieved if there is a sense of commitment
among implementing agencies and the State Governments. The Committee recommends that
sincere efforts should be made to ensure that whatever investment is made for the development
of NER should yield concrete result so much so that the outcome should manifest itself
(Para 7.6 ibid)
2

3
Action Taken
1.2.2 The Ministry has noted the recommendation of the  Committee for future guidance. It has
strengthened its monitoring mechanism to ensure mat the implementation of projects lead to
achievement of desired objectives. Detailed monitoring formats have been evolved for area
inspection by officers allotted to each state, as area officers.
Further Recommendation
1.2.3 The Committee would like to underscore that strengthening of monitoring
mechanism for the projects in the NE Region is absolutely essential. As natural corollary,
the monitoring formats that have been evolved should be strictly adhered to.
1.3 NON-LAPSABLE CENTRAL POOL OF RESOURCES (NLCPR)
Recommendation
1.3.1 The Committee feels that the efforts made by Ministry of DoNER to persuade Ministries/
Departments to change their norms according to the condition of the NER have not yielded the
desired results. The Committee recommends that more vigorous efforts need to be made by the
Ministry of DoNER so that more and more Ministries/Departments change their norms in respect
of their flagship programmes and spend the allocated amount in the NE. (Para 8.6 ibid)
Action Taken
1.3.2 This Ministry has taken up with those Ministries, whose unspent balances form major part
of the NCPR, to amend norms for incurring expenditure on their flagship schemes, as per condition
of the North East, so as to ensure that these Ministries are in a position to spend 10% their GBS
in the North East Region.
1.4 NON-LAPSABLE CENTRAL POOL OF RESOURCES (NLCPR)
Recommendation
1.4.1 The Committee views with concern the fact that even though DoNER had projected
Rs.12 crore for NLCPR, only Rs.650 crore has been allocated for the current financial year. The
Committee also took note of the fact that for NLCPR the projection was made on the of
performance during the last two years. The Committee further notes the unspent balance lying with
other Ministries. The Committee therefore recommends that the allocation for NLCPR may be
increased appropriately at RE stage to meet the requirement of various projects proposed to be
taken up by the Ministry. The Committee also recommends that allocation may also be made from
out of the unspent balance of various Ministries. The Committee desires that the Ministry of
DoNER may peruse the matter at highest level for early release of the funds. (Para 8.13)
Action Taken
1.4.2 M inistry has already taken up with the Planning Commission for higher allocation of funds.
Discussions are at presently going on at the highest level.
Further Recommendation
1.4.3 The Committee reiterates its recommendation that the Government should consider
making budgetary allocation to the Ministry of DoNER as per its requirement so that the
projects undertaken should not remain incomplete for want of funds. .

4
1.5 NON-LAPSABLE CENTRAL POOL OF RESOURCES (NLCPR)
Recommendation
1.5.1 The Committee is constrained to observe that the State Governments could not complete 233
projects within the time schedule mainly due to the delays in utilization of funds and limited
working seasons. The Committee is however not convinced by the reasons for the backlog in
completion of projects. The Committee strongly recommends that the State Governments should
strictly adhere to the time schedule in this regard (Para 8.14 ibid)
Action Taken
1.5.2 Considering the delay in completion of projects under NLCPR, Hon’ble Minister had written
to the Chief Minister of North Eastern States on 16.05.2008 requesting their personal attention to
this vital matter to expedite completion of the projects sanctioned under NLCPR. Ministry of
DoNER regularly reviews the progress of projects and pursues with the States regularly.
1.6 NORTH EASTERN COUNCIL
Recommendation
1.6.1 The Committee takes a critical view of the allocations made for NEC. The allocation of
Rs. 624 crore in BE 2008-09 as compared to the allocation of Rs. 600 crore in the previous year,
is in no way commensurate with the number of projects to be taken up by NEC. Besides the new
projects, the NEC has also several spilled over projects. The Committee is in agreement with the
view that it is difficult for NEC to fulfil its role as a regional planning body due to financial
constraints. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the NEC may be provided with suitably
enhanced allocation at RE stage so that NEC projects which are facing difficulties due to shortage
of funds do not get affected. (Para 9.10 ibid)
Action Taken
1.6.2 M inistry has already taken up with the Planning Commission for higher allocation of funds.
Discussions are at presently going on at the highest level.
Further Recommendation
1.6.3 The Committee reiterates its recommendation that the Government should consider
making budgetary allocation to the Ministry of DoNER as per its requirement so that the
projects undertaken should not remain incomplete for want of funds.
1.7 ADVOCACY AND PUBLICITY
Recommendation
1.7.1 The Committee takes note of the reply given by the Ministry that media campaign will be
operational soon. The Committee would like to be apprised of the activities to be undertaken under
the media plan. The Committee recommends that efforts should be made to achieve the objectives
of the strategy in right earnest. The Committee is also of the view that whatever steps that are
being taken under ‘Advocacy and Publicity’ and its results are still not visible. It feels that there
must be inherent weaknesses and problems in the plans being made. In the present age of
globalization, efforts should be made to bring the North-East Region into the mainstream of the
country at the earliest and for that Advocacy and Publicity is the most effective medium. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that renewed thrust may be given on media campaign and it
should be effectively used (Para 10.9 ibid)

5
Action Taken
1.7.2 A Media Campaign by the Ministry has been finalized and will be launched by the Ministry
in the current year, which includes newspaper advertisements and TV commercials on various
themes like natural beauty, tourism, investment opportunities, cultural uniqueness, developmental
work of the Central Government etc., radio jingles/spots, sponsored features in Newspapersl
Magazines, arranging panel discussions on TV etc.
1.8 NERAMAC
Recommendation
1.8.1 The Committee recognizes the fact that the North East Region, though industrially backward
due to poor infrastructure, has great potential in terms of agriculture, horticulture, floriculture. This
potential of the region has remained unharnessed and here the NERAMAC comes into the picture
which could accelerate the growth in these sectors. The Committee expresses its disquiet over the
fact that the Ministry in general and NERAMAC in particular are not able to tap the potential
available in abundance and this shows poor planning and initiative. Sincere efforts are required
to be made to harness these resources. The Committee recommends that the pineapple juice
concentrate plant in Tripura may be revived by providing it better machineries and skilled
manpower. (Para 13.8 ibid)
Action Taken
1.8.2 It has been decided to re-structure and modernize the pineapple juice concentration plant of
NERAMAC at Nalkata (Tripura) under NLCPR scheme. Detailed project report in this regard has
been received and is being processed for funding of the project.
1.8.3 Besides the above project, following initiatives have been taken for strengthening of
NERAMAC:—
Diversification of existing pineapple juice concentration plant in Tripura to a multi-fruit
processing unit.
Setting up a multi-fruit processing Unit at Silchar in Assam.
Setting up a Central Quality Assurance and Packing unit with common brand for marketing
of processed products from the North East.
Setting up of one more cashew processing plant of 4 tons per day capacity in Mankachar
in Assam.
1.8.4 The Corporation has opened its branch office in every State of the North East Region to
widen and improve its operations. It has tied up with North Eastern and Handicrafts and Handloom
Development Corporation Ltd. (NEHHDC) to broadbase market for NE products
1.9 PROMOTION OF TOURISM AND HOSPITALITY
Recommendation
1.9.1 The Committee is of the considered view that the NE region has a great potential to become
an attractive tourist destination in the country particularly for eco and adventure tourism. If the
tourism potential of the region is to be fully tapped, sufficient infrastructure and peaceful
environment should be in place at the earliest. Moreover, tourism in NE provides a large number
of employment opportunities. The eco-tourism not only provides livelihood for local communities

6
and adds importance to local traditions and cultures, but also generates substantial revenue for
environmental conservation and management. The Committee is pleased to note that in the proposed
BE 2008-09, an amount of Rs. 9 crore has been allocated for Tourism which is an increase of
79.64% from the last year. (Para 15.9 ibid)
Action Taken
1.9.2 As a follow up action on the recommendation of the Fourth Sectoral Summit on Tourism
and Hospitality Sector, a Tourism Conclave was held to attract LTC Tourists to the NER. This
followed issuing of relaxation to travel to NER by Air even to those who are otherwise not entitled
to travel by air and also convert their Home Town LTC into anywhere in India specific to NER.
In the month of June and July this facility generated a huge tourism activity and visits of
Government employees to Sikkim, Assam, Meghalaya and other States in the Region. This activity
is expected to pick up in the coming festive season. This facility is upto 2009-10. Other efforts
are also being made by holding information sharing seminars and workshops with all stakeholders.
1.10 PROMOTION OF TOURISM AND HOSPITALITY
Recommendation
1.10.1 The Committee appreciates the several initiatives including Media Campaign and involving
the private sector for development of the tourism sector, taken by the Ministry. However, a lot more
is yet to be done and a lot of investment is required to develop tourist infrastructure in the NER
to make it one of the most attractive tourist destination not only in the country but in the world
as well. The Committee desires that a long-term perspective plan and a roadmap may be prepared
for creation of better tourism infrastructure on a fast track basis as it is the main hurdle in the
way of development of tourism sector in the region. (Para 15.10 ibid)
Action Taken
1.10.2 The Government is making all possible efforts for improving and upgrading infrastructure
in the North East Region by adopting PPP mode to make it feasible and accelerate the speed. In
this regard, IL&FS is setting up chain of budget hotels in the Region. This will be a significant
step for promoting tourism in the Region.
1.10.3 NEC has also taken up concrete steps in developing infrastructure in the North East Region.
Some important projects undertaken are as follows:
1. More than 7700 kms of roads constructed.
2. Bridge over the Brahmaputra at Tezpur and bridge over Barak River at Raniferry Ghat,
Silchar.
3. Support to the rail-cum-road bridge over the Brahmaputra at Jogighopa.
4. Funding of upgradation of 10 (ten) airports in the region including the LGB
International Airport at Guwahati.
5. Improving air connectivity through support to Alliance Air for procurement of 4
(four) 50 seater aircrafts for operation in NE Region.
6. Inter-State Bus Terminus at Guwahati and Silchar in Assam and Dimapur in Nagaland.
7. Eight Transmission Lines 1285.50 Circuit KMs. Another 369 Ckt.Kms. of Transmission
Lines are being supported and the work is in progress and expected to be completed
by the end of 2009.

7
8. NEC, in collaboration with the IL&FS, is helping in establishing of budget hotels in all
the NE States for promotion of Tourism; one Yatri Niwas in Guwahati is also coming
up.
Further Recommendation
1.10.4 Even though Home Town LTC has been allowed for travel to NER, but the Committee
has been given to understand that several government employees could not utilize this
facility due to lack of sufficient flights and hotels/guest houses. Therefore, Government
needs to look into these aspects. The Committee has been given to understand that in
several parts of North Eastern States, helicopter services are available to compensate the
lack of road, rail and air link. However, as Central Government’s LTC Rules have no
provision for reimbursement of expenditure incurred on journey performed by helicopter,
Central Government employees are unable to avail the helicopter facilities for visiting
various parts of North Eastern Region. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
Government may examine this aspect and make necessary provision in the LTC Rules for
the reimbursement of expenditure incurred on journey performed by helicopter by the
Central Government employees.
1.11 CONNECTIVITY
Recommendation
1.11.1 ‘Connectivity’ within the NE Region is of utmost importance if this region is to be brought
into the political, social and economic mainstream of the country. The Committee is of the considered
view that Government should adopt a proactive approach and should be diligent in implementing the
various policy initiatives. This area should be given topmost priority in the scheme of governance
of the NER and special impetus be pr ovided wherever needed. (Para 16.10 ibid)
Action Taken
1.11.2 Connectivity is given utmost importance by the Ministry of DoNER and NEC. More than
60 percent of NEC’s budget is committed to the transport and communication sector. Till now,
with the support of NEC, about 7700 Kms. of roads have already been constructed.
1.11.3 Steps have also been taken to improve air connectivity by supporting upgradation of existing
10 airports in the NER with the help of Airports Authority of India (AAI). These are located at
Guwahati, Tezpur, Agartala, Silchar, Dimapur, Lilabari, Imphal, Jorhat, Dibrugarh, Shillong.
Feasibility studies for upgradation of non-operational airports at Kailashhar and Kamalpur in Tripura,
Along, Daparijo, Ziro, Pasighat and Tezu in Arunachal Pradesh, Tura in Meghalaya have also been
taken by the Airports Authority of India. Efforts are being made to have a dedicated airline in North
East.
1.11.4 Efforts for increasing the rail network in the North East Region have also been taken by
Ministry of Railways. At present it is minimal and constitutes only 4% of the total rail network of
the country. The Ministry of Railways has been spending more than 10% of their GBS in the
region. Presently, work is in progress on 14 projects, which include eight new lines, 5 Gauge
Conversion and 1 Doubling of line.
1.12 CONNECTIVITY
Recommendation
1.12.1 The Committee recommends that development of proposed three Greenfield airports at

8
Itanagar, Cheithu and Pakyong should be given priority. The Committee desires that the proposal
regarding two new Greenfield airports at Tawang and Kokrajhar be examined expeditiously. The
Committee is pleased to know that the agreement between NEC and Alliance Air has been extended
for the year 2008 for operating ATR services between locations in the North East. The Committee
desires that airports at Silchar, Dibrugarh and Umroi may also be upgraded at the earliest. It
should be impressed upon the AAI to submit its DPR on non operational airports, namely,
Kailashahar, Kamalpur and Pasighat and DPR on Tezu airport, as early as possible.
(Para 16.12 ibid)
Action Taken
1.12.2 The Greenfield Airports at Itanagar, Cheithu and Pakyong will be constructed by the AAI
with direct funding from the Planning Commission. Feasibility report on the Tawang Airport has
already been submitted by AAI and the Airport has been found feasible. The report has been sent
to the Planning Commission for considering the same for preparation of the DPR. As per the
feasibility study carried out by the AAI it has been found that the airport at Kokrajhar is not
feasible. AAI has recommended upgradation of Rupsi airport in lieu  of Kokrajhar, Rupsi being quite
close to Kokrajhar. The State Government has accordingly been requested to confirm whether
upgradation of Rupsi is acceptable to them.
1.12.3 Further, the airports at Silchar, Dibrugarh and Umroi (Shillong) are already under
up-gradation. At Silchar, modification of terminal building, installation of the Doppler VHF (Very-
High-Frequency) Omnidirectional Range (DVOR), strengthening of apron and taxi way and V-Sat
have already been completed whereas strengthening and extension of runway is under progress. At
Dibrugarh, installation of Remote Area Business Message Network (RABMN), V-Sat and VHF
Receiver have already been completed, while the construction of terminal building is under
progress. Extension of runway and associated works, although planned, could not be taken up
because of problems of land acquisition. At Umroi Airport, installation of DVOR has already been
completed while up gradation of airport including runway extension and terminal building are under
progress. AAI has submitted pre-feasibility report for Kailashahr and Kamalpur. The Airports have
been found feasible and the Planning Commission has been requested to grant in-principle approvals
for the same. Detailed Project Reports for Pasighat and Tezu Airports have been received and are
being processed.
Further Recommendation
1.12.4 The Committee recommends that the Greenfield Airports at Itanagar, Cheithu and
Pakyong may be taken up at the earliest as it could help boost development in the region.
The Committee also recommends that the upgradation work proposed at other airports, may
be completed without further delay.
1.13 NORTH EAST INDUSTRIAL AND INVESTMENT PROMOTION POLICY (NEIIPP) 2007.
Recommendation
1.13.1 The Committee is pleased to note that several incentives have been taken for new industrial
units as well as the existing ones in the NEIIP, 2007. While appreciating the initiatives to attract
foreign investment in the region, the Committee feels that more emphasis should be given on
potential investors from other parts of India. However, in order to give fillip to the NEIIPP, 2007,
the Committee recommends that the Ministry of DoNER should interact with the Ministry of Micro,
Small and Medium Enterprises for promoting enterprises including agro and rural industries. The
Committee strongly feels that the benefits accruing from Micro Small Medium Enterprises
Act, 2005. Khadi and Village Industries Act, 2007 and North East Industrial and Investment

9
Promotion Policy, 2007 would go a long way in promoting MSMEs in the region provided adequate

the Government should give high priority to the problem of connectivity in the region as without

organized by NEDFI who have been given the role of distributing various kinds of subsidies under
the policy. CII and ICC Kolkata have also held informatics exchange programmes in the North East
Region and Kolkata to promote investment in the region. Indian Institute of Entrepreneurship
(IIE), Guwahati, an institute working under Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises
(MSME) is working to make, would be investors, aware of provisions and relaxations under the
NEIIEP-2007. In this connection, a meeting was held in the middle of June, 2008 with

products, Cane and Bamboo Cluster at Aizwal; for cane and bamboo, Nagaland; Beed making
Cluster in Mon district, Nagaland. As regards infrastructure, specially road connectivity, it is being
taken care of under Special Accelerated Road Development Programme of Department of Road
Transport and Highways, PMGSY of Ministry of Rural Development and also though NLCPR.
1.14 INITIATIVES UNDER INDIA’S LOOK EAST POLICY
Recommendation
1.14.1 The Committee recognizes that under India’ s Look East Policy, border trade with
neighboring landlocked countries is of utmost importance as the North East Region could provide
a link between India and South East Asian countries for increasing trade between the two regions.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the ‘Look East Policy’ may be followed up vigorously
in close coordination with other concerned Union Ministries and State Governments. As pointed out
by the Secretary, Ministry of DONER, the infrastructure of the Land Customs Stations needs to be
improved for better border trade. (Para 19.4 ibid)

Policy vis-a-vis the North East with the concerned Ministries/organizations and State Governments.

Ministry of External Affairs has opened a Branch Secretariat in Guwahati as part of the initiatives
under the Look East Policy and North East India. A chapter on Look East Policy: the North East
Perspective has been included in the NER Vision 2020 document. Ministry of DONER also actively
participates in discussions and consultations organized by the Ministry of External Affairs with the
countries that neighbour North Eastern India.

Recommendation

overall development of the region. The Committee feels that the schemes for development of

10
transport infrastructure, industrial base, agricultural and allied sectors with special emphasis on
medicinal plants in the region should be given prominence in the Vision NER, 2020. The Committee
hopes that the Vision document would give a direction to the development process in the region.

of this Vision Document. (Para 20.3 ibid)

2.1 TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE AND CAPACITY BUILDING
Recommendation
2.1.1 The Committee is happy to note that 36 students have been selected for training in
Commercial Pilot Licence (CPL) and Aircraft Maintenance Engineering (AME) and some young
persons have also been selected for airhostess training. The Committee however, wishes to observe
that these trainings are being held outside the North-Eastern region. If the North Eastern region
has to be strengthened and the capacity for the region has to be upgraded, such Institutes should
be opened there instead of sending people outside for training. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that an early decision may be taken on starting the Pilot Training Institute at Lilabari.
Whatever problems that are coming in the way be sorted out at the earliest and the Central Ministry
may take initiative in this regard. The Committee is of the view that there is huge potential for
fashion designing and fashion technology in the North East which is still to be tapped. The
Committee reiterates that a National Institute of Fashion Technology may be opened in the North
East at the earliest. The Committee is also of the view that there is a huge potential for
sportspersons in the North East and this potential has not yet been tapped. To tap this potential,
a separate Sports Institute or Sports Academy is required in the North East. The Committee,
therefore, reiterates that a Sports Academy may be opened in the North Eastern Region:
(Para 11.7)
Action Taken
Pilot Training Institute
2.1.2 In principle, approval for setting up the Pilot Training Institute at Lilabari, Assam has
already been granted on the 30th January 2006 by the Ministry of Civil Aviation. The
techno-feasibility study was assigned to M/s Foundation for Aviation and Sustainable Tourism
(FAST), New Delhi and they submitted the draft report. Certain clarifications and supplementary
information sought from FAST have been received and FAST have been asked to submit the final
report. The main issue is related to the availability of instructors who are in short supply in this
country and the difficulties in attracting them to a remote location like Lilabari. Government of
Assam has identified a plot of land measuring 75 bighas near Lilabari for the purpose and is
awaiting the clearance of the Land Advisory Committee. The NEC is constantly pursuing the matter
with the Government of Assam. The institute is proposed to be established on a Public Private
Partnership (PPP) mode. The draft Expression of Interest for inviting bidders has been sent to the
Ministry of Civil Aviation for their comments and vetting. An outlay of Rs 399.00 lakhs have been
kept in the Annual Plan 2008-09 for the purpose.
National Institute of Fashion Technology
2.1.3 The National Institute of Fashion Technology is an autonomous institute under the Ministry
of Textiles, Government of India. They decided to open a NIFT Centre in Shillong and have sent
the DPR to the Ministry for funding. The matter is in progress.
11

12
North East Adventure Sports Academy
2.1.4 Ministry has taken up with Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports to find out how many
institutes/academies have been set up by them in each State of  the North East Region, to see
whether this Ministry also needs to establish an Adventure Sports Academy in the region.
Further Recommendation
2.1.5 The Committee expresses its concern over delay in setting up the Pilot Training
Institute at Lilabari, Assam. The Committee feels that issue of availability of instructors
should be sorted out at the earliest. The Committee further desires that the Ministry of
DoNER may expedite the process of getting land use clearance from the Land Advisory
Committee, Government of Assam, for the purpose. The Committee recommends that the
Government should expedite the process of opening a NIFT Centre in Shillong. The
Committee also recommends that the Government may take up on priority, the opening of

Recommendation

Recommendation

Protocol and Kaladan River multi-modal transport route from Mizoram to Sittwe Port should be

2.5 POWER SECTOR
Recommendation
2.5.1 The Committee is of the view that there is an immense potential of hydro-power in the
region which has still not been fully harnessed. The Committee recommends that the emphasis
should be laid on completion of on-going projects without further delay before new projects are
taken up in the Eleventh Plan. (Para 21.6)
Action Taken
2.5.2 Hydro Power Potential for Mega and Major Projects at 60 % load factor has been assessed
for the country as 84000 MW, out of which 31857 MW (38%) is available in the North-Eastern
Region. This vast potential has yet to be tapped for utilization. Only 3.4% of the potential available
in NE (31857 MW) has been harnessed so far. Hence, ample scope exists in this region for
harnessing Hydro Power Potential in a sustainable manner.
2.5.3 The North Eastern Council has played a major role in the economic upliftment of the region
through infrastructure development in the power sector. In 1981, the installed Capacity of the

15
North Eastern Region was 410 MW only. In the last two decades, the total installed capacity has
increased to more than fivefold at 2033.12 MW, (as on April 2008) excluding Sikkim which
comprises of both Hydro and Thermal segments. Augmentation in Generation capacity of North
East has been made possible by ensuring active involvement of the North Eastern Council. The
NEC since its inception has contributed 673.50 MW of capacity addition (630 MW Hydro and
43.50 MW thermal).
2.5.4 Small/Mini Hydel projects with a total capacity of 4.5 MW have also been taken up on
viability gap funding basis by NEC, so far, in conformity with NEC’s Pasighat Proclamation on
Power. The projects are targeted to be completed by the end of 2010. An amount of Rs. 4.00 crore
has been released till date and the work is under progress.
2.5.5 21MW Baramura Gas Based project Unit-V , in Tripura at project cost of Rs 80.00 crore is
the only on-going Thermal Power project taken up and funded by North Eastern Council. An
amount of Rs 30.00 crore has already been released by NEC till date. The project is scheduled to
be completed in 20 months i.e. by end of the year 2009 and the executing Agency is the Tripura
State Electricity Corporation Ltd.
Further Recommendation
2.5.6 The Committee is unhappy to note that even though out of total hydropower
potential of 84000 MW in the country, 38% (31857 MW) is available in NE region, but out
of it only 3.4% of this has been tapped so far. The Committee recommends that all the
ongoing hydro power projects may be completed without further delay. The Committee
recommends that the ongoing thermal power project “21MW Baramura Gas based project
unit-V” in Tripura funded by North Eastern Council be completed within the stimulated
time-frame.
2.5.7 The Committee further recommends that the Government should explore in a big
way “Public Private Partnership Model” for tapping the huge potential of hydro-power
available in NE.
2.6 EDUCATION
Recommendation
2.6.1 The Committee feels that there is some mismatch in the figures pertaining to literacy and
dropout rates in the NE States. The Committee therefore recommends that the figures should be re-
checked/verified by the concerned authorities so as to get the true picture in this regard. Regarding
shortage of teachers in NE States, the Committee recommends that the Two Years’ Certificate
Course in Teachers’ Training offered by IGNOU through the distance learning mode, may be
availed of effectively for training of existing teachers. At the same time setting up of new teacher
training institutes may also be considered. The Committee is optimistic that the revised funding
pattern of 90:10 will give a boost to Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan in the NE Region. (Para 22.5 ibid)
Action Taken
2.6.2 The matter has been taken up with the Ministry of Human Resource Development for
ascertaining the correct number of dropouts in each of the North Eastern States and to initiate
remedial measures for reducing the number of these.
2.6.3 In response to this Ministry’s request to initiate measures for reducing the shortage of
teachers, Ministry of HRD has intimated that shortage of faculty is a national problem being faced

16
by the higher education sector both in the Universities, and Colleges and Technical Institutions. It
has taken following steps to alleviate the problem at national level, including NE Region.
(a) Retirement age of teachers has been increased from 62 to 65 years for teaching
staff;
(b) Where considered appropriate retired teachers have been permitted to be
re-employed;
(c) For teaching graduate students M.Phil qualification is now considered sufficient and
for post-graduate classes Ph.D. is adequate and exemption from passing next
examination has been granted as a temporary measure;
(d) The State Governments and other institutes have been requested from time to time
to expedite filling up of vacancies without enforcing any ban orders;
(e) For attracting students to do Ph.D. the fellowship amount has been increased
considerably;
(f) A Pay Revision Committee has been appointed by UGC for making recommendations
regarding revised pay scales for university teachers keeping in view the need to
attract and retain competent faculty in teaching posts.
Further Recommendation
2.6.4 The Committee notes that the response of the Ministry to its specific recommendation
regarding setting up new Teachers’ Training Institutes in the NE, is evasive. The Committee
urge upon the Ministry to initiate immediate action in a time-bound manner.

REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT HA VE NOT BEEN RECEIVED
3.1 Transfer of Hill Area Development Programme (HADP) and Border Area
Development Programme (BADP)
Recommendation
3.1.1 The Committee expresses its deep concern that even though the two programmes i.e. Hill
Area Development Programme (HADP) and Border Area Development Programme (BADP) are
shown in the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961 against the Ministry of
DoNER but the programmes are yet to be transferred to it. The Committee is constrained to note
that inspite of its recommendation in the One Hundred and Twenty Seventh report, the Cabinet
Secretariat has not taken any steps in this direction. The issue is pending with that Secretariat since
long. The Committee reiterates that such important issue should be resolved on priority basis.
(Para 14.4 ibid)
Action Taken
3.1.2 The matter is being taken up with Ministry of Home Affairs/Cabinet Secretariat to take a
view on the issue.
Further Recommendation
3.1.3 The Committee fails to understand why the Government is dragging its feet in the
matter. The Committee would expect that Government would come out with a clear view in
the matter without any further delay.
3.2 PROMOTION OF TOURISM AND HOSPITALITY
Recommendation
3.2.1 The Committee desires that the Ministry in tandem with the Ministry of Home Affairs and
the Ministry of Tourism should expedite the issue of relaxing the movement of tourists in the North-
Eastern region in the interest of development of NER and tourism. (Para 15.11 ibid)
Action Taken
3.2.2 Ministry of Development of North Eastern Region had taken up with the Ministry of Home
Affairs, the issue of relaxation of Protected Area Permit/Restricted Area Permit (PAP/RAP)
restrictions. Ministry of Home Affairs has informed that in the case of Arunachal Pradesh, orders
for relaxation of P AP/RAP restrictions have been issued in May 2008. Proposals from the States
of Mizoram, Nagaland, Manipur and Sikkim are under consideration.
3.3 ROPEWAY AT TAWANG
Recommendation
3.3.1 The Ropeway Project at Tawang is a classic example of procrastination. The Committee
17

18
expresses its displeasure over the fact that the foundation for the Ropeway was laid by the
President of India in 2002 yet the progress of construction of this ropeway is not at all satisfactory.
Even though funds were allocated last year, it is a matter of concern that the State Government
was in the process of issuing tenders in August 2007. It is unfortunate that the Secretary could not
give the latest status of the project. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the
Ministry must take suitable initiatives and follow-up action to ensure completion of project without
further delay. Otherwise, the Committee apprehends that there would be time and cost overrun.
(Para 17.4)
Action Taken
3.3.2 The construction work at the site of the project has already started and work relating to
foundations of the towers is going on. The State Government has been advised to accelerate the
pace of the implementation of the project and submit latest physical/financial progress of the
project.

REPORT
CHAPTER-I
THE SCHEME OF MODERNISATION OF PRISON ADMINISTRATION
1.1 Background
1.1.1 Explaining about the historical background and the genesis of the scheme of Modernization
of Prison Administration, the Ministry of Home Affairs in the background note submitted in April,
2007, stated that keeping in view the pathetic, unhygienic and awful condition of the average Indian
Prisons primarily because of overcrowding, Mulla Committee (1983) ♣, Kapoor Committee
(1986) ♦, Iyer Committee (1987) ♥ and Parliamentary Committee on Empowerment of Women
(2001)♠ recommended for replacement of dilapidated prisons; improvement of living conditions;
provision for medical and psychiatric services; vocational training and gainful employment;
diversification of educational programme; improvement in the condition of women prisoners;
segregation of prisoners; provisions for free legal aid and speedy trials including humane and
dignified treatment with the prisoners. In compliance with the recommendations of these
Committees, the Government of India released a fund to the tune of Rs. 125.24 crore during 1987-
2000. However, conditions of the prisoners did not improve as per expectations nor was there any
significant change in the general conditions of prisons or in the attitude of the jail authorities.
1.1.2 The M inistry further stated that ‘prison’ being a State Subject as per Entry 4 of List II (State
List) to the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution, the upkeep of prisons was within the jurisdiction
of the State Governments. Due to paucity of funds with the State Governments and keeping in view
the awful condition of the prisons in the States, the Kapoor Committee, especially, emphasized the
need to provide Central Assistance to the States under the scheme called the Modernisation of Prisons
for improving the conditions of the prisons, prisoners and prison personnel.
1.1.3 Considering the appalling condition of the prisons in the States, paucity of funds with the
State Governments and the dire need for improving the conditions of prisons, prisoners and prison
staff, a much larger investment in this sector was required. Based on an assessment conducted by
the Bureau of Police Research and Development (BPR&D), the Central Government launched the
scheme of Modernisation of Prison, Administration. The Ministry of Home Affairs in the
background note stated that the non-plan scheme “Modernisation of Prison Administration” with a
total outlay of Rs. 1800 crore was launched by the Central  Government. The scheme involved
the contribution from the Central Government as well as the State Governments on a cost sharing
basis of 75:25 and was proposed to be implemented over a period of five years from 2002-03 to
2006-07. The scheme is applicable to 27 States except Arunachal Pradesh to whom Eleventh
Finance Commission had granted Rs. 10 crore separately for building a jail.
♣ All India Jail Reforms Committee of 1980-83 under the Chairmanship of Justice Anand Narain popularly known as the
Mulla Committee, to study all aspects of prison administration in the country and to advise measures for its effective
improvement.

1.1.4 According to Model Prison Manual for the Superintendence and Management of Prisons in
India, formulated by BPR&D, Ministry of Home Affairs, closed prisons are classified into three
categories, as under:—
(a) Central Prison: authorized population not to exceed 1000.
(b) District Prison: authorized population not to exceed 500.
(c) Sub-Jail: authorized population not to exceed 300.
1.1.5 The Ministry further stated that the scheme envisaged preparation of five years perspective
plan and annual action plans for each year by the States and their approval by Central Empowered
Committee. The Five Years Perspective Plan and Annual Action Plan 2002-03 were obtained from
the State Governments and approved by the Central Empowered Committee. As the scheme was
launched in the middle of the year 2002-03, no budget provision was earlier made and the
requirement of Rs. 270 crore as Central share for the year was made in March, 2003 through a
supplementary demand at a much later stage. Accordingly, the release of Central share to States
aggregating Rs. 270 crore in the first year was released in March, 2003.
1.1.6 The Ministry further stated that due to delayed start, the Scheme virtually started in the
third year, and was therefore extended by a further period of two years w.e.f. 1.4.2007 without
affecting the total outlay of Rs. 1800 crore. The State Governments had also been allowed to utilize
10% of their entitlement under the Annual Action Plan 2006-07 on purchasing equipment for
modernization of jails and building/improving infrastructure for undertaking correctional
programmes.
1.1.7 The Ministry stated that the primary objective of the scheme was to assist the States in
enhancing the prisons’ capacity for accommodating prisoners and to improve the living conditions
of inmates and prison staff. The scheme aims at extending basic amenities, medical and psychiatric
services, better security, vocational training programmes, rehabilitation of prisoners, improving the
conditions of women prisoners and facility for the care and primary education for their children.
1.1.8 Under the scheme, financial assistance is given to State Governments for undertaking the
following items of works:—
(i) Construction of additional jails to reduce overcrowding;
(ii) Repair and renovation of existing jails;
(iii) Improvement in sanitation and water supply; and
(iv) Living accommodation for prisons staff.

CHAPTER-II
OFFICIAL PRESENTATION BY THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS
2.1.1 During the course of presentation made before the Sub-Committee, the Joint Secretary,
MHA stated that although the primary responsibility was with the State Governments to take
necessary action for modernizing infrastructure of prisons, with a view to bringing the prison
management in consonance with the philosophy of reformation and rehabilitation in place of
deterrence and retribution, the Scheme for Modernization of Prison Administration was introduced
by the Central Government due to paucity of funds available with the State Governments. It was
also stated that elaborate measures had been taken to monitor the implementation of the scheme
which inter-alia included submission of quarterly progress reports by the State Governments,
extensive review meeting periodically with each State Government and regular visits by the senior
officers of MHA to States.
2.1.2 Explaining about the Scheme, the Joint Secretary, MHA informed the Sub-Committee that
the following measures were taken for an overall prison reforms:—
(i) Insertion of new section 436A  in the Code of Criminal Procedure which provides
that where an undertrial prisoner, other than the one accused of an offence for
which death has been prescribed as one of the punishments, has been under
detention for a period extending to one half of the maximum period of imprisonment
provided for the alleged offence, should be released on a personal bond with or
without sureties;
(ii) Section 436(1) in the Code of Criminal Procedure has been amended to provide that
if a person is accused of a bailable offence and cannot furnish surety, the Court shall
release him on a personal bond without sureties;
(iii) A system of plea bargaining has been introduced where an accused will be entitled
to a reduced sentence if he admits to the crime and agrees to compensate the victim;
(iv) Proposal for amendment in the Code of Criminal Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 2006,
whereby in Section 167, following sub-Section(2) is to be inserted
♣:—
“no Magistrate shall authorize detention of the accused in custody of the police
under this section unless the accused is produced before him in person for the first
time and subsequently every time till the accused remains in the custody of the
police, but the Magistrate may extend further detention in judicial custody on
production of the accused either in person or through the medium of electronic video
linkage.
Provided further that in case of woman under eighteen years of age, the detention
shall be authorized to be in the custody of a remand home or recognized social
institution.”
(v) Approval has been given for creation of 1562 Fast Track Courts upto 31 March, 2010.
So far 10.4 lakh cases have beet disposed off;

(i) Prisons do not have budget of their own.
(ii) The Prison Act, 1894, which is still in use, needed to be amended.
(iii) The Annual Conference of DGs (Prisons) should be held at fixed intervals on the

(iv) The P rison Act, 1894 does not come in the way of implementing ‘Model Prison Manual’.
(v) The adoption of the ‘Model Prison Manual’ by states would solve many problems

(vi) States like Punjab are going at a very slow pace in regard to modernization of

(x) NCRB records should be checked to know the performance of State Governments.
(xi) The Committee should ask the states to clarify as to whether they were abiding by

CHAPTER-III
VISITS TO JAILS
3.1 The Sub-Committee visited some selected jails in the country to make on the spot study
of the implementation of the scheme. The Sub-Committee visited Tihar Jails in Delhi on
21st September, 2007. The Sub-Committee also visited Haryana, Punjab, Chhattisgarh, Orissa,
Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. The Sub-Committee, during the study visits, also
held discussions with the senior officers of the jails and the State Governments. The details of the
discussions and the findings of the Sub-Committee are given in the succeeding paragraphs.
3.2 Visit to Tihar Jails, Delhi
3.2.1 The Sub-Committee visited Tihar Jails, Delhi on 21st September, 2007. The sub-Committee
visited Central Public Relation Office at Gate No. 3, Model Interview Room, IGNOU Study Centre,
Jail Hospital and Drug de-addiction Centre in Jail No. 3, Jail Factory in Jail No. 2. The Sub-
Committee also visited Meditation Room, TIP Room in Jail No. 4 besides a creche in Jail No. 6.
3.2.2 It was apprised that the erstwhile Delhi Jail, located in Delhi Gate area, was shifted to Tihar
Village in the Western part of Delhi in 1958. In the beginning, only one Central jail was
commissioned, but as on date, there were ten functional jails in Delhi-nine Central Jails in Tihar
Campus and one District Jail at Rohini.
3.2.3 During the course of the visit and the interaction with the inmates and the officials of the
prison, the Sub-Committee came across following facts:—
(i) There was overcrowding of inmates in various jails. The total lodging capacity of all
the Nine Central Prisons and District Jail, Rohini is 6250 prisoners whereas there
were 12884 prisoners lodged in the jails as on 17th September, 2007;
(ii) A large number of under-trials, almost 81% of prisons population, are lodged in the
jails. There were undertrials who are unable to furnish surety after the grant of bail;
(iii) The lodging of high security prisoners including dreaded terrorists, pose serious
problems to the jail administration and its management;
(iv) About 8 to l0 per cent of the prisoners are drug addicts and their management
through Drug Detoxification and Rehabilitation Centers was itself a big task. There
should be compulsory testing of HIV/AIDS of all inmates;
(v) A drug De addiction Centre with a capacity of 120 beds is not fully functional due
to shortage of medical officers and other para-medical staff. A proposal for additional
requirement of 54 medical and para-medical staff has been forwarded to Government
of NCT of Delhi;
(vi) The jail administration is facing acute problem due to shortage of staff in various
ranks. Around 25% of posts of the total sanctioned strength of 1154 are vacant. The
ideal requirement of the prison staff as per the Model Prison Manual should be in
the ratio of 1:6. A proposal has been sent to Delhi Government for creation of 16
posts of Deputy Superintendents and 78 posts of Assistant Superintendents in Delhi-
Jails for their smooth functioning;
6

7
(vii) There is no training institute to train the prison personnel in various aspects of prison
management. The present system of training being imparted to the staff for three
months at Patiala is inadequate;
(viii) Adequate rehabilitative schemes should be introduced for the convicts who are
released from the prisons after undergoing imprisonment for five years or more.
Provision of assistance of Rs.10,000/- to the life convicts by the Social Welfare
Department is totally inadequate;
(ix) A proposal was sent to GNCT of Delhi for upward revision of wages paid to the
prisoners on the scale of Rs.52/- for the skilled, Rs.44/- for the semi-skilled and
Rs.40/- for the unskilled per day;
(x) The process of acquisition of land and its allotment to the Prison Department by
DDA at Narela and Baprola has not been completed;
(xi) There are complaints of atrocities and inhuman torture by the prison staff in tandem with
domineering prisoners, meted out to the first time prisoners. There is lack of medical
facilities in the prison hospital and the behaviour of the Doctors is also not proper.
3.2.4 The Sub-Committee after holding discussion with inmates and officials of the jail
administration and of the Government of NCT of Delhi, was constrained to note that there were
several vacancies in the prison staff. The sub-Committee directed them to take necessary action
to fill up the vacant posts expeditiously and also sanction new posts for which proposals have
already been sent. The Sub-Committee also observed that most of the present incumbents were
promotees, in the age group of 56-59 years and not capable of withstanding the high-stress
assignment and unable to exercise effective supervision and control in managing the Prison affairs.
The Sub-Committee directed that necessary steps should be taken to post young and dynamic
officers as Jail Superintendents for effective and meaningful management of Jails.

had been brought under control with the help of local administration and police. It was also
informed that the jail was one hundred years old, spread in an area of 8.6 acres. The jail was
meant for only a few inmates. However, there were 590 prisoners against a capacity of 385.

prisoners and most of them were involved in dowry related cases. There were two female
warden’s-while one was permanent, the other was temporary. The Sub-Committee also interacted

3.30.1 The Sub-Committee, during its visits to various jails in different States, noted the common

(i) Need for increasing literacy among the prisoners, facility of correspondence courses

jobs after release.

new jails should be constructed.

including HIV/AIDS, etc.
(v) Due to lack of sufficient police escorts, undertrials are often not taken to the courts
on the due date which results in their prolonged detention.
(vi) Improper functioning of workshop in the prison.
(vii) The wages given to the prisoners for working in the prison workshops, etc., is very
less. They should also have the option of working extra hours.
(viii) T elephone facility is not available to the prisoners. This leads to illegal use of mobile
phones, etc. Telephone facility be provided for inmates in the presence of a jail staff
on a trial basis;

(ix) Poor undertrials do not get sufficient financial help to defend their cases in the
courts. Public Prosecutors need to be given better payment for motivation  to take

(xviii) Improvement in V isitor’s chamber with intercom facilities as already functioning in

(xix) Consultation with a recognized dietician for preparing a proper healthy diet menu for
prisoners.
(xx) Large areas of land of the almost all jails are lying unutilized, which could be better

(xxi) A nexus between jail officials and inmates leading to prevalence of contraband drugs

(xxii) Complaints of atrocities and inhuman torture by the prison staff in tandem with

4.3.1 The Sub-Committee during its visits to various jails has found that one of the most
important hurdles coming in the way of prison reforms is the problem of overcrowding of
prisoners which is the root cause of most of the ills besetting the prisons. This problem
could be solved only by construction of additional barracks and new jails on priority basis.

The Ministry of Home Affairs should seriously introspect and discuss this aspect with all the
State Governments before launching the second phase of the Scheme.
4.4 Lodging of inmates as per their classification
4.4.1 The Committee has been given to understand that the inmates in the prison are classified
and lodged on the basis of sex, age, gravity of crime, undertrial/convicts. During its study visits
to various States, the Sub-Committee found that the first time offenders were being kept with
hardened criminals in the prisons and it could lead to their involvement in further criminal activities.
When this was brought to the notice of the Ministry, they replied as under:
“Prison is a State subject as per List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution and
the responsibility of prison administration lies primarily with the respective State
Governments. Therefore lodging of inmates in the jails as per their classification is done
by the respective State Governments. However, the Model Prison Manual  prepared by the
Government of India also prescribes segregation of inmates on the basis of their age, sex,
gravity of crime etc.”
4.4.2 The Committee is disappointed with the routine reply of the Ministry. Although
‘Prison’ is a State subject, the Committee feels that the Ministry should take the initiative
for ensuring that the State Governments comply with the Model Prison Manual. The
Committee is of the considered view that the young offenders/undertrials need to be kept
separately as it has been observed that, when they are kept with other hardened criminals,
they often commit more serious crimes after release from Jails. The Committee desires
that serious action may be taken to address this issue.
4.5 Section 436A of Cr. P.C. and Plea Bargaining
4.5.1 Section 436A of the Criminal Procedure Code provides that where an undertrial prisoner
other than the one accused of an offence for which death has been prescribed as one of the
punishments, has been under detention for a period extending to one half of the maximum period
of imprisonment provided for the alleged offence, should be released on a personal bond with or
without sureties. It also provides that in no case will an undertrial prisoner be detained beyond the
maximum period of imprisonment for which he can be convicted.
4.5.2 Section 436(1) of Cr. P.C. has been amended to the provide that if a person is accused of
a bailable offence and cannot furnish surety, the Court shall release him on a personal bond without
sureties. There is also a mechanism of plea bargaining in which an accused will be entitled to a
reduced sentence if he admits to the crime and agrees to compensate the victim.
4.5.3 When asked about the status report on implementation of the provisions for mandatory
release of undertrial prisoners under Section 436A and 436 (1) and Plea Bargaining under
sections 265 to 265L of Cr. P.C., to reduce the pendency of cases in Courts, the Ministry replied
as under:
“Although ‘Prison’ is a State subject, the Home Minister has written to all the Chief
Ministers on 11th September, 2007 apprising them of the various reform measures initiated
by the Central Government with a request to accord the highest priority in implementing

4.5.4 During its study tour to various jails, the Sub-Committee found that many poor
prisoners were languishing in jails despite being granted bail due to their inability to provide
surety. The Committee feels that the State Governments have not been able to effectively
invoke Sections 436A, 436(i) and 265 to 265L of the Cr. P.C., 1973 with the objective to
reduce the overcrowding and languishing of undertrials in jails. The Committee urges upon
all the concerned authorities to extensively use these legal provisions which would help in
reducing the burden on the prison infrastructure.
4.6 Model Prison Manual
4.6.1 In pursuance of the directions of Supreme Court in a case “Ramamurthy Vs. State of
Karnataka”, Bureau of Police Research and Development prepared a Model Prison Manual for the
superintendence and management of Prisons throughout the country which was circulated by the
Ministry of Home Affairs to all States/UTs for its adoption. Asked about the status of
implementation of Model Prison Manual in order to maintain the uniformity of working of prisons
through-out the country, the Ministry, in its written reply, stated as under:
“The Model Prison Manual was circulated to all the States on 31.12.2003 for adoption.
The Andaman and  Nicobar Island has adopted the manual fully. The States such as Andhra
Pradesh, Gujarat, Haryana, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Mizoram, Punjab, Sikkim, NCT Delhi
and Pudducherry have already responded to the suggestions given in the Model Prison
Manual. During the visits to various jails by the representatives of the Ministry, it has been
observed that the  provisions of the Model Prison Manual are being implemented by the
States with suitable local changes/modifications” .

25
4.6.2 Contrary to the claim of the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Sub-Committee, during
its study visits to the various States, found that the Model Prison Manual was not being
implemented properly. The Committee, therefore, desires that the Ministry should impress
upon the State Governments to implement the Model Prison Manual in its letter and spirit
so as to maintain uniformity in the prison administration throughout the country which will
go a long way in effecting prison reforms.
4.7 Conditions of women prisoners
4.7.1 There are instances when women inmates had been harassed sexually by the prison staff.
It has also been seen that women prisoners face social ostracism after coming out of the jail and
the stigma of jail term sometimes ruins a women’s life because her family usually refuses to take
her back after her release. Separate prisons for women are not available in all the States. They are
generally housed in segregated wings of prisons for men. The situation of children accompanying
their mothers inside the jail is also a cause of concern. The sub-Committee during its study visit
found that the facility of creche for these children was not available in some of the jails.
4.7.2 The Supreme Court has expressed its deep concern on the plight of children who are lodged
in prisons with their mothers and has issued thirteen guidelines in the case of R.D. Upadhayay Vs.
State of Andhra Pradesh (Writ Petition Civil 559 of 1994) for implementation by all the States/UTs
and State Legal Authorities ensuring the extension of certain facilities to the women prisoners and
their accompanying children, with the direction to comply with these directives within four months
from the date of issue of the order and file compliance report by the individual State. The
Parliamentary Committee on Empowerment of Women after undertaking a study on the subject
“Condition of Women Prisoners” had in its third report emphasized the need to provide facilities such
as creches for children of women prisoners kept in jails, hygienic living conditions and provisions
for separate kitchens for women prisoners, etc. Responding to the issue, the Ministry stated that:—
“the Scheme for Modernisation of Prisons includes construction of new jails, repair and
renovation of existing jails, construction of staff quarters and improving the water and
sanitation in jails. The State Governments had the flexibility of building creches, and
separate kitchens for women in the new prisons to be constructed and under the repair and
renovation component. It was also stated that depending on the requirement States like
Assam, Madhya Pradesh, Punjab etc. had used the funds for the above purpose.”
4.7.3 T he Committee takes note of the disappointing reply of the Ministry. The guidelines
for the preparation of action plan by the individual States lay down specifically that all the
States will have at least one prison exclusively for women. The States which do not have
prison exclusively for women have to plan for the construction of at least one such prison
with the capacity depending upon the average number of women prisoners in the respective
State. The guidelines also lays down the requirement of creation of infrastructural facilities
like creches for the accompanying children of women prisoners, hygienic living conditions
and provision of separate kitchen for women prisoners. The Committee feels that the State
Governments should be advised to give priority to construction of separate women jails,
repair and renovation of existing women jails and provision of facilities such as creche for
minor children lodged with their mothers; and hygienic living conditions for the children
and separate kitchen for women prisoners.
4.8 Sanitation, water supply, health and hygiene in prisons
4.8.1 The prisons in India face the problem of water supply, sanitation and hygiene and lack of
health care facilities. The overcrowding in the jails has further aggravated these problems and in
many jails, living conditions are deplorable.

26
4.8.2 The Sub-Committee during its study visit, found that the jails at Karnal (Haryana), Ludhiana
(Punjab) and Raipur (Chhattisgarh) were lacking in proper toilets and bathroom and were
inadequate to cater to the daily needs of the prisoners. The prisoners at Raipur jail complained of
low supply of water. According to the guidelines for the preparation of action plan by the individual
States, there should be one toilet per 10 prisoners, 100-150 litres of water per prisoner per day
and adequate arrangement for storage of water in each ward. The guidelines also say that water
harvesting may be included as an essential component of all prison buildings. The Sub-Committee
during its study visit also found that many jails were lacking proper medical facilities and many
prisoners complained of lack of proper attention by the doctors and medical staff. The Sub-
Committee was also given to understand that there were instances when sick prisoners needing
emergency medical attention were not provided the same due to unavailability of police escort.
4.8.3 The Sub-Committee also observed that the inmates were being shaved by the barber using
same set of blades which could lead to spread of HIV/AIDS and other infection among the prisoners.
4.8.4 The Committee strongly recommends that concern of health and hygiene in the
prisons should be urgently addressed for which adequate supply of water and proper
sanitation facilities were a must. It also recommends that the existing medical facilities in
the prisons should be overhauled and one police escort party should always be provided to
accompany a prisoner requiring emergency medical attention. In the second phase of the
scheme, proper emphasis may be laid on this aspect. The Committee feels that at least in
the newly constructed additional barracks and jails, facilities for water harvesting,
alternative sources of energy, converting garbage into bio-gas etc. must be provided. The
Committee is also of the firm opinion that the old system of shaving should be dispensed
with and each prisoner should be provided a separate disposable rajor to check the spread
of HIV/AIDS among the prisoners.
4.9 Visitors' Room
4.9.1 The Sub-Committee was informed that chances of malpractices were very high when
visitors (Mulaqaatis) (friends and relatives) come  to meet the inmates. At that time they happen to
be emotionally charged and their emotions/sentiments which are exploited by the staff/members of
the prisons posted there. During its study visits, the Sub-Committee observed that the visitors’
rooms and associated areas of activity were neglected by the authorities and due to presence of
a large number of persons in that area, the inmates were not able to talk to their visitors-properly.
4.9.2 The Committee recommends that steps should be taken to make the procedure of
visits to jail inmates transparent in all the prisons of the country and there should be a
mechanism to get the feedback from the relatives of the inmates. The Committee strongly
recommends that modern visitors’ chamber should be constructed in place of ramshackled
ones in which there would be transparent glass facade and intercom facilities so that the
prisoners’ visitors can talk while looking at each other.
4.10 Other related issues
4.10.1 Prison, as per the modern concept, is a correctional centre where undertrials and individuals
convicted for a crime are confined and usually deprived of a range of personal freedom. Keeping
an individual in isolation from society in itself is a major punishment for any crime which he/she
has allegedly committed. So, the modern sociological consideration demands that the condition of
life in the prison should not be miserable and its environment should be humanized. The idea of
“humanization” does not mean making prisons a comfortable place to which every prisoner would
like to return after release but only treating inmates as human beings. The condition of prisons in
our country is widely viewed as extremely wretched.

27
4.10.2 It is the considered opinion of the Committee that the conditions in an average
Indian Prison are awful, which present a very depressing picture. Being overcrowded,
unhygienic and gloomy, these incarceration centers are presumed to be places far from
being any kind of correctional centre. They often breed hardened criminals who practically
become a menace to the society. A mindless adherence to centuries old jail manuals leaves
very little scope for any innovative approach in the matter of dealing with people who end
up in prisons for various reasons and under various circumstances. With revolutionary
changes taking place in every field around us, it is high time that our mindset towards
prisoners also undergoes a change, that a prison should truly reflect the spirit of correction
and reformation by treating the inmates as human beings.
4.11 Telephone facility for inmates
4.11.1 The Committee recommends that telephone facility should be provided in some
selected prisons of the country on a trial basis. The inmates could use this facility in the
presence of a jail staff. The telephonic conversation could also be taped which would help
in tracking the connections of the hardened criminals. In the opinion of the Committee,
telephone facility for inmates could check illegal use of mobile phones in the prisons.
4.12 Prison Workshops
4.12.1 The Committee observed that barring a few prisons, the prison workshops were still
of primitive type. In these workshops activities like carpet making, carpentry, etc. were still
being done. The Committee recommends that prison workshops need to be urgently
modernized and they should function like small modern industrial units with latest
equipments. The Ministry may look into this aspect in the second phase of the scheme.
4.13 Wages of Prisoners
4.13.1 The Committee is of the firm opinion that daily wages of the convicted prisoners
working in the prison workshops need to be increased. Simultaneously, these prisoners
should also be given the option of working extra hours to earn more money. The Committee
also desires that undertrials should be given an opportunity to work in the prison workshop,
if they willingly agree to do so.
4.14 Vocational Training
4.14.1 The Committee desires that there should be an effort to achieve total literacy among
prisoners across the country. The Committee, therefore, recommends that there should be
facility of correspondence courses in vocational disciplines in the prisons and degrees/
diplomas should be awarded to the prisoners after successful completion of their course so
that they could lead a normal life in the mainstream of society, after their release.
4.14.2 The Government may consider opening of ITI-like institutions within the jail
premises to impart industrial training in various disciplines to the inmates, which would go
a long way in rehabilitating them after their release. In this context, the State authorities
can also consider converting existing prison workshops into ITIs.
4.15 Grievance Redressal System
4.15.1 The Committee is of the opinion that a grievance redressal mechanism should
properly function in every jail in the country and there should be transparency in its
functioning. The Committee, therefore, suggests that every State Government should
introduce “Mobile Petition Box” for prisoners to give suggestions and complaints.

28
4.16 Vacancies
4.16.1 The Committee is of the considered opinion that the existing vacancies of prison staff must
be filled up expeditiously and new posts for which proposals have already been sent, be created
at the earliest. The Committee also feels that the duties and responsibilities of Jail Superintendents
are of a very sensitive nature requiring high degree of commitment, discipline and good physical
fitness. Under the Jail Manual the Superintendent of a Jail is the back-bone of the entire supervision
and governance of a particular jail. Most of the present incumbents are promotees, in the age group
of 56-59 years and not capable of withstanding the high-stress assignment and unable to exercise
effective supervision and control in managing the Prison affairs. The Committee recommends that
State Governments should be advised to post young and dynamic officers as Jail Superintendents
for effective and meaningful management of Jails.
4.17 Open Jail
4.17.1 During its study visits the Sub-Committee observed that ‘Open Jail’ was a prison of a new
kind where prisoners having good conduct and who had spent satisfactorily a certain portion of
their sentence, were kept. In this prison, the prisoners were allowed to live a community life and
enjoy much freedom during their stay in the jail. The Sub-Committee also visited open jails near
Bhubaneshwar and Hyderabad. The inmates of the prisons were very well behaved. In the open
prison near Bhubaneshwar, the land was being utilized properly for growing medicinal and aromatic
plants by using biological farming practices. The Superintendent of this prison informed that the
vegetables and other eatables produced in the jail were consumed by the prisoners and the surplus
was sold in outside market. The factory workshop in the prison was functioning properly.
4.17.2 The Committee feels that every State should have such open jails where the
prisoners having good conduct and who have spent considerable years of their sentence,
could be sent.
4.18 Release of Prisoners Sentenced for Life
4.18.1 D uring the course of their study visits, the Sub-Committee found that there were many
poor convicts who have completed fourteen years of term with a good conduct but as they were
unable to pay bribe, the officer in-charge of the respective police station, the latter would give
negative reports and consequently the State Sentence Revisory Board would not consider their
cases for release.
4.18.2 The Committee recommends that the power of giving character certificate entrusted
to be respective Jail Superintendents as they are the authorities who had been closely
watching the activities of the inmates for a long time.
4.19 Horticulture in Jail Premises
4.19.1 The Sub-Committee came across the large tracts of land in the jails which remained
unutilized. The Committee feels that planting of medicinal plants, horticulture and kitchen
garden etc. should be encouraged in such land as it would not only increase the income of
the prisons but would also lead to improving the physical environment in the jail premises.
4.20 Drugs in Jail Premises
4.20.1 During the study visits to various jails, the inmates complained to the
Sub-Committee about the nexus between officials of the jails and some inmates resulting
in the supply and use of drugs inside the jails. The Committee takes a serious view of this

29
and strongly recommends that necessary steps should be taken by each of the State
Governments and the prison officials to prevent such a nexus and use of drugs in jails.
4.21 General
4.21.1 The Sub-Committee noticed and came across several problems in the jails visited by
it. All the problems have been explained in the preceding chapters. The Committee desires
that the concerned jails and the State Governments and also the Union Ministry of Home
Affairs may look into those problems and solve them at the earliest.
4.21.2 As stated elsewhere in this Report, the condition of most of the jails in the country
leave much to be desired and require a complete change of mindset of those providing
administration to these prisons. The ideals of reformation and resettlement should be a
predominant feature of reforming the inmates in a democratic society. The purpose of the
present Report would be more than achieved if it attracts the attention of the concerned
quarters in the administrative machinery and this modest effort is continued further to
ensure that our country has prisons of global standards with all basic and primary facilities
for the inmates.
